The UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermaths of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement.

"The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement.

UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV."

UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light.

"In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find."

UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars, however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas.

Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas.

This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life.

UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge.

Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon.

So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged.

Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves. Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate.

The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope.

"With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events."

UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers.

"We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds."

All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover.

"Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #770. Dolly Parton Sings ‘Her Heart Out’ on Posthumous U2 Collaboration ‘Torn’: Stream It Now

Co-written by U2, Parton and Snow Patrol's Johnny McDaid, "Torn" is the country great's last recorded vocal performance.

Dolly Parton always gave it her all across her glittering, extraordinary career. At the stroke of midnight, the country music icon reminded us of what we’re sorely missing with the release of “Torn,” Parton’s posthumous collaboration with U2. Explore Bono Dolly Parton U2 See latest videos, charts and news

The duet between Dolly and U2 frontman Bono is the closing song on Carnaval De Luz (which translates to “Carnival of Light”), the Irish rock band’s sixteenth and latest studio album. Related Aria Vega Wins Best New Artist at the 2026 Latin Grammys: 'Dreams Know No Fear' On Winning First Latin Grammy, Camila Fernández Thanks Expectant Baby for 'Strength to be Here' 50 Cent Trolls Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Affair With 'P.I.M.P.' Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It'

Co-written by U2, Parton and Snow Patrol‘s Johnny McDaid, “Torn” is the country great’s last recorded vocal performance, and it connects the full 24-track deluxe version of the project, followed in sequence by the surprise-release EPs Days of Ash and Easter Lily, as a double album.

Dolly pulls it together, to create a spiritual whole. “You sense a border crossing,” Bono remarks in a statement. “And so you move from the south into the north, and you have Dolly Parton singing to you as you cross the border.”

Carnaval De Luz is the first album of new material from U2 in nine years. To celebrate its release, Island Records shares several versions of the country-tinged “Torn,” including the “Kent Wells Version” and the “T Bone Burnett Take,” all of them featuring the unmistakable voice of Dolly.

Speaking ahead of its release, Bono told Rolling Stone that the recording was, admittedly, almost too difficult for him to hear.

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song,” Bono remarked. “And you can hear that. And I can’t even listen to it now.”

Parton recorded her vocals for “Torn” in June, just two months before her passing. Bono was blown away by her talents. “She sang her heart out,” he told RS, “and I cannot believe that’s an 80-year-old woman.”

Parton approved the final mix before her passing Aug. 25 at 80 from a brief battle with cancer.

“It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure,” Bono explained to Rolling Stone. “The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”

Carnaval De Luz drops 50 years after drummer Larry Mullen Jr. pinned a handwritten notice to the message board of Mount Temple Comprehensive School in Dublin, with the fateful message: “Drummer Seeks Musicians To Form Band.”

What happened next is the stuff of legend.

With their political hearts exposed on their collective sleeves, Bono, The Edge, Mullen and Adam Clayton would become arguably the world’s biggest band in the second half of the 1980s, a crown they managed to wear well into the ‘90s despite the explosion of grunge, indie, alternative rock, hip-hop and electronic dance music.

The band has sold 175 million albums, according to Island Records, and bagged 22 Grammy Awards. Along the way, they landed 34 songs on the Billboard Hot 100, including two leaders, along with eight No. 1s on the Billboard 200 chart. Induction into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame came in 2005.

U2 had the honors of being the first band to play the Sphere in Las Vegas, which they inaugurated in September 2023 with the residency, U2:UV Achtung Baby Live at Sphere.

According to reps, the fourpiece is currently working on plans to translate the new album for Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show On Earth World Tour, a live tour in 2027.

Stream U2’s “Torn” featuring Dolly Parton and the new album Carnaval De Luz.

#769. Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. New research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders

An estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

"As more people recognize how important sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," said Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next."

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward important information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," said Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments."

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions showed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

However, an important question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team plans to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

#767. Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

The basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information. They are linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions from Parkinson’s and Huntington’s disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction.

Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is described in a collection of 26 papers published in Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron. The research includes understudied neurons1, provides insights about how some brain cells change with age2 and suggests which might be linked to diseases3.

The atlas, a collaboration between hundreds of scientists in nine countries, is part of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) — a US$500-million project launched in 2022 by the US National Institutes of Health aimed at creating reference maps of mammalian brains.

“It’s a massive dictionary that we needed in the field,” says Ana Muñoz-Manchado, a neuroscientist at the University of Cádiz in Spain, who studies the basal ganglia in neurodegenerative disorders.

The basal ganglia atlas contains 21 million cells from the brains of six humans, three million cells from three rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, and 1.5 million cells from two marmosets4. The researchers also used data from previously published maps of the whole mouse brain5,6.

By comparing the basal ganglia between the primate species, the researchers identified 61 cell types in humans, macaques and marmosets that have been conserved over 76 million years3.

The team analysed brain tissue samples from different developmental stages across the lifespan of the species. The latest work combines information about these cells in unprecedented detail, from measurements of their gene expression and DNA modifications that control gene regulation to recordings of their electrical activity, as well as how DNA is folded inside their nuclei.

The researchers also mapped where each cell is located in the brain and designed a common framework to characterize and annotate the cells. It is “essentially a scaffold on which we can now fairly readily complete the rest of the brain”, explains Michael Hawrylycz, a bioinformatician at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who took part in the project.

One study examined 1.1 million cells in the basal ganglia’s largest structure — known as the striatum — from 19 deceased human donors7. Unlike many other brain areas, the striatum has no neat anatomical boundaries. The researchers identified six zones in the human and macaque striatum with distinct molecular signatures, each containing distinct populations of neurons and glial cells.

“The cells in these zones all look the same under the microscope, but have very strong transcriptional differences and are strikingly consistent from person to person,” said co-author Evan Macosko, a neurobiologist at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in a press release from the institute.

Macosko and his colleagues also found that gene expression patterns that distinguished each zone from the other became increasingly similar with age, particularly in brain regions affected by Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease.

Another study analysed nearly four million cells in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from 178 deceased adult donors between the ages of 27 and over 902. The researchers found that the cellular make-up of the two brain regions varied between people, particularly for non-neuronal cells known as glial cells. This underscores the need for brain cell atlases to account for these individual differences.

#766. Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Every human body produces carbon dioxide simply by converting food into energy. Although the amount released by one person may seem small, the combined output of billions of people adds up to an enormous quantity.

A new study led by the University of Bath estimates that carbon dioxide production from human metabolism increased by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons annually. The researchers found that the dramatic rise was primarily the result of population growth, rather than a substantial increase in how much CO2 each person produces.

The findings could help scientists better understand the global carbon cycle, which describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and land. By measuring humanity's contribution more accurately, researchers hope to improve predictions about how well efforts to reduce carbon emissions will work.

Why Human CO2 Emissions Are Different From Fossil Fuels

Despite the enormous numbers, the researchers emphasize that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism is fundamentally different from the emissions generated by burning fossil fuels.

When people breathe out CO2, most of that carbon originally came from the food they consumed. Plants absorbed it from the atmosphere relatively recently, meaning it is already circulating through the natural carbon cycle.

Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is different. These fuels contain carbon that has remained trapped underground for millions of years. Burning them releases that long-stored carbon into the atmosphere, adding to the amount of CO2 circulating through the Earth's climate system.

The new research, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, was led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the University of Bath's Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism.

The team calculated that global CO2 production from human metabolism climbed from 1.18 billion metric tons in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons in 2015. More than 60% of that increase could be attributed to the growing number of people worldwide.

"We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven't had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

"What we've found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be."

How Scientists Measured Humanity's CO2 Production

To estimate how much carbon dioxide people generate, the researchers analyzed thousands of measurements collected from individuals across the human lifespan, from infants to older adults.

These measurements provided information about the CO2 produced by the body during ordinary daily activities. The team then combined those findings with worldwide population figures and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic CO2 production had changed over time.

The results showed that population growth was the dominant factor behind the 74% increase. Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide generated by individual people played a much smaller role.

Accurately measuring this process is important because human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment. Its influence on local carbon measurements can be especially noticeable in densely populated cities and urban areas, where large numbers of people live and work close together.

Understanding these contributions can help researchers develop more complete carbon budgets, which track the sources, movements, and destinations of carbon within the Earth's systems.

Scientists Stress That Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change

Although the study reveals a surprisingly large amount of CO2 production, its findings should not be interpreted as evidence that human breathing is a major cause of global warming.

The researchers are not recommending that people reduce their physical activity or change their diets to lower the carbon dioxide produced by their bodies. Instead, the goal is to make scientific measurements and calculations of the global carbon cycle more accurate.

Distinguishing between carbon dioxide produced through natural biological processes and carbon released by burning fossil fuels is essential for understanding the planet's changing climate.

Professor Gonzalez emphasized this distinction:

"The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We're not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

"What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs."

By establishing a clearer picture of humanity's metabolic CO2 production, the researchers have provided another piece of information scientists can use to track global carbon movements and evaluate strategies for reducing emissions.

This dazzling collection of ancient stars could hold clues to the Milky Way's past.

The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange.

But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed.

The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity.

Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old!

Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell.

Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history.

Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

#763. Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot

Scientists have achieved a new world record by producing extraordinarily intense X-ray flashes that last just 300 attoseconds, an almost unimaginably brief period of time. Using the European XFEL, a powerful X-ray research facility, the team concentrated the flashes into an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair.

By squeezing so much X-ray energy into such a tiny space, the researchers created an exceptionally powerful beam that could open new possibilities for studying the behavior of electrons inside atoms and molecules. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists observe the rapid movements of electrons during chemical reactions and potentially even learn to control them.

The experiment took place in April 2026, and the findings have now been published in the scientific journal Optica.

Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes Last Just 300 Attoseconds

"This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse," says Ichiro Inoue from the University of Tokyo, first author of the publication.

Hard X-rays are a form of light with extremely short wavelengths. Scientists use two measurements to describe their extraordinary power. Fluence refers to the amount of energy delivered to a particular area, while intensity also considers how quickly that energy is delivered.

In this experiment, each X-ray pulse lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds (an attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second). Such incredibly short flashes offer researchers a way to investigate events that unfold far too quickly for conventional observation.

To concentrate the X-rays, the team used a specialized optical arrangement called an advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez, or AKB, system. It consists of two exceptionally precise mirrors that focus the beam in different directions. Each pulse underwent four reflections in total, with one mirror focusing the X-rays vertically and the other horizontally.

The result was an astonishingly small focal spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers (a nanometre is a billionth of a meter). By directing the energy into this microscopic area, the researchers were able to achieve record-breaking intensity.

"A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL," says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. "But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter."

These nonlinear interactions occur when extremely intense X-rays cause matter to respond in ways that would not normally happen under weaker illumination. Studying such effects could reveal new details about how atoms and electrons behave under extreme conditions.

An Extraordinary Reaction Inside Copper Atoms

To confirm the exceptional intensity of their X-ray pulses, the researchers directed them at a thin sheet of copper. The experiment provided independent evidence that the focused flashes reached peak intensities exceeding 10²⁰ watts per square centimeter.

When the X-rays struck the copper, they knocked electrons out of the atoms' innermost electron shells, leaving behind empty positions known as 'holes'. Electrons from other parts of the atoms then moved into these vacancies, releasing energy in the form of X-ray light.

Under ordinary circumstances, this emitted light travels in many different directions. However, when the incoming X-rays become sufficiently intense, something remarkable happens. The emitted light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to release additional X-rays traveling in the same direction, producing an amplified beam.

Scientists call this phenomenon amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

"It is almost magical to see this happening," says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument, where the study was conducted. "Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction."

The team also observed another important signature of extreme intensity. As they increased the energy of the X-ray pulses, the amplified signal initially became much stronger. At higher energies, however, the increase slowed and eventually leveled off, a behavior known as saturation.

This pattern is expected only under exceptionally intense X-ray illumination. Its appearance provided additional confirmation of the record intensity calculated from the pulse energy, duration, and size of the focused beam.

A New Way to Explore the Hidden World of Electrons

Beyond setting a world record, the breakthrough could significantly expand scientists' ability to investigate some of nature's fastest processes.

Electrons play a central role in determining how atoms bond together, how molecules interact, and how chemical reactions unfold. Their movements happen on extraordinarily short timescales, making them difficult to observe directly.

By combining ultrashort X-ray flashes with extremely high intensity, researchers hope to capture information about electrons before the incoming radiation has time to substantially alter the material being studied. This could provide a clearer picture of electron behavior inside atoms and molecules and, in the longer term, potentially lead to methods for influencing electron motion during chemical reactions.

The advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror system used for the record-setting experiment was transported from Japan. European XFEL is now preparing to receive its own AKB system, with delivery expected in early 2027.

The new equipment is being funded through a collaboration with the University of Hamburg, with additional support from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR).

Once the system has been installed and commissioned, scientists from around the world using the MID instrument are expected to gain access to these exceptionally brief and intense X-ray flashes. The upgraded capabilities could allow researchers to investigate electron behavior at a level of detail that has previously been difficult to achieve, bringing them closer to understanding and potentially controlling the fundamental processes behind chemical reactions.

#761. ‘Ebenezer’ Reviews Roundup: Johnny Depp’s Comeback Gets a Chilly Reception

Critics are very split on Ti West's 'A Christmas Carol' adaptation, calling Depp everything from a "soulless worst Scrooge ever" to "eminently redeemable."

Nearly every critic reviewing Ebenezer seems to be finding their way around the same question: How do we feel, exactly, about Johnny Depp starring in a major studio film once again?

Conveniently, Ti West‘s adaptation of A Christmas Carol provides plenty of metaphorical fodder given it’s a redemption tale, after all, with Depp’s Scrooge given lines like, “I am not the man I was!” and “I was once good, and I know I can be again!”

Still, many critics aren’t sold on the film — or Depp, for that matter, with the actor once again buried in makeup and prosthetics. The film currently has a 51 percent positive score on Rotten Tomatoes, and even the positive reviews tend to be a bit tempered (it will be interesting to see if the audience score for Ebenezer is significantly higher, as critics assigned to cover the film might very well feel more negatively towards Depp than fans). The movie’s supporting cast — including Rupert Grint, Ian McKellen, Andrea Riseborough, Daisy Ridley and Tramell Tillman — are largely drawing praise. Related Stories Movies 'Ebenezer' Review: Johnny Depp Gets a Creepily Effective Comeback Vehicle in Ti West's Horror-Tinged Take on Dickens' Yuletide Classic Movies Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer': First Reactions

Here is a sampling of reviews from major publications. Ebenezer opens Friday (watch the final trailer below).

The Hollywood Reporter: “Johnny Depp really needed a comeback vehicle, and he’s found an effective one in Ti West’s horror-tinged adaptation that allows the actor to deliver the sort of quirky theatrical performance for which he became famous. While Ebenezer doesn’t break any new ground, other than possibly being the first version of the story not really suitable for young children, it fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status … Depp … delivers a performance that no one would call subtle. In style, it most closely resembles a heavily made-up Albert Finney’s broad take on the character in the now largely forgotten 1970 musical Scrooge. But the actor’s charisma and star power eventually come through.”

Vulture: “Johnny Depp is the worst part of Ebenezer, but he’s also the reason it exists, so it’s futile to try and separate his presence from the rest of the movie, which is, inconveniently, pretty good. Depp is also doing a tiresome variation on the mugging that’s become his primary approach to acting ever since the role of Captain Jack Sparrow vaulted him into Disney-franchise levels of fame — a vaguely comic, scenery-chewing mode that doesn’t fit in with the rest of the movie…West’s interpretations of the spirits who visit the miser over the small hours of the night are imaginatively spooky, especially the Ghost of Christmas Past, played by Andrea Riseborough as a kind of corpse bride clad all in white with rheumy eyes.”

The New York Times: “It’s an attempt to, as much as one can in one role, play the hits. Whether consciously or simply out of a lack of creativity, the aging star is playing an agreeable version of himself, more than anything, aimed at providing a fond reminder of the Depp-in-drag iconography he crafted for himself over the last few decades … Ebenezer implicitly markets itself on the empirically shaky idea of a beloved Depp that was taken away. If you don’t squint too hard, his Scrooge might not only function as a return, but a memory wipe.”

The Times UK: “It’s just a shame, then, that the film around him, directed by the horror film-maker Ti West (Pearl, X), is hugely uninspired and has little to offer the already swollen canon of Christmas Carol adaptations. The Alastair Sim version from 1951, the Bill Murray comedy from 1988 and the Muppet musical reboot from 1992 are all vastly superior to this surprisingly vanilla take. … But really this is just a chance for audiences to see that Depp, like the character he is playing, is eminently redeemable and ready again, in the strongest possible terms, for his close-up.

Boston Globe: “Under all that makeup, Depp is easily the worst Scrooge I’ve ever seen. His performance is a soulless, hollow shell, never once convincing us of Scrooge’s miserly rage or his ultimate redemption. There isn’t an ounce of humanity in this performance; it may as well have been generated with AI.”

The Guardian: “As Scrooge himself, Depp is in fact rather good; theatrically bad-tempered and petulant and, as with his Jack Sparrow, I suspect Depp’s comedy timing and sonorous British accent might have been learned from his old Fast Show comrade Paul Whitehouse. He is better at the unredeemed Scrooge than the saved version at the end, where some of the abject pathos is missing. This is a decent enough new version, avoiding any big new revisionist takes which might have clunked.”

Slashfilm: “With the exception of a small moment here and there, Depp’s Scrooge is largely solid yet unremarkable. Which begs the question: why bother in the first place? It seems like the entirety of Ebenezer was arranged to allow Depp to chew scenery and showboat around, which the actor perversely refuses to do. It’s possible that Depp now considers such an approach something he’s no longer interested in, and it’s not like he hasn’t given grounded performances before, like his turn as John Dillinger in Public Enemies, for example. Depp’s performance as Scrooge simply doesn’t feel fully realized.”

IndieWire: “While Depp has never been the subtlest of actors, his post-Sparrow pivot away from artistic curiosity has distended his talents into such a grotesque caricature of their former charm that Ebenezer left me feeling like I may never be able to empathize with his screen presence again … Given the emphasis the director puts on the film’s genre spin, it’s ironic and surprising that Ebenezer is at its best when it focuses on the most basic human elements of its story, if only because the supporting characters offer such a welcome contrast to whatever Depp is doing.

The Daily Beast: “Ebenezer has enough commendable qualities to justify its existence, and Depp sturdily balances Scrooge’s nastiness, silliness, and, finally, kindness … Not fresh enough to become a classic, but with enough scariness to unnerve its younger viewers, West’s latest is a competent, accurate retelling fit for the Yuletide season—and, perhaps just as crucially, a Depp vehicle that suggests the beleaguered star isn’t ready to relinquish his A-list status just yet.”

The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground.

Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027.

"Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher."

Rocket Lab is best known for Electron, a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO).

Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO.

Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control).

Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30.

The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s.

"The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said.

That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket. For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO.

The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful.

But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which can haul more than 100 tons to LEO.

There's a real worry among folks in the space community that this massive payload capacity won't be available to them for a while. SpaceX has made it pretty clear that early Starship operations will be geared toward internal priorities — specifically, the buildout of SpaceX's Starlink V3 broadband network and its Starmind AI data-center constellation.

These will be very big jobs, even for the most powerful rocket ever built. For example, the Starlink V3 megaconstellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk. Starship can carry about 60 of these spacecraft to LEO per launch, so just building out the constellation will require about 1,700 liftoffs.

The numbers for Starmind will be even more mind-boggling, for SpaceX wants that constellation to eventually harbor a million satellites.

The coming launch bottleneck should increase demand for Electron as well as Neutron, Beck said during Monday's call. After all, many small-satellite operators have launched with SpaceX over the years, booking spots on Falcon 9 "rideshare" flights. And those opportunities are now drying up.

"The next logical alternative is of course an Electron, so we see tremendous traction there," Beck said.

#758. Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined

Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track - both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning from the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO), Department of Biology at Aarhus University, senior author of the study.

Challenging the Myth of Europe's Ancient Forests

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements.

Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover.

These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.

What 23 Million Years of Evidence Reveals

To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years.

Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch (which began around 23 million years ago) through the pre-industrial era.

Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.

These included fossilized pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal left by ancient wildfires, and chemical signatures preserved in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals. The researchers also examined fossil insects and mammals, along with ancient environmental DNA recovered from sediments.

Environmental DNA consists of genetic material left behind by organisms in their surroundings. When preserved in ancient deposits, it can help scientists identify plants and animals that lived in an area long ago.

Together, these different sources of evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct not only what types of vegetation existed, but also how ecosystems changed over time and how animals influenced their surroundings.

"Each type of proxy offers its own perspective, but together they let us see whether the landscapes were covered by dense forests, open grasslands, or a mix of the two. By combining these datasets across time - from the Miocene to the pre-industrial era - we could trace long-term changes in vegetation and the role of large herbivores with much greater confidence than earlier studies that used only one method," explains the study's lead author, ECONOVO PhD student Szymon Czyzewski of Aarhus University.

The evidence points to a consistent pattern. Across more than 20 million years, Europe's landscapes were typically a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces, and flowering plants rather than continuous stretches of closed forest.

Importantly, these mixed landscapes were not limited to one particular climate. They existed under temperate conditions comparable to those in much of Europe today, as well as during warmer and colder periods.

Elephants, Rhinos, and Bison Shaped Europe's Wilderness

One of the most striking findings concerns the influence of large wild herbivores.

Ancient Europe was home to animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs, and bison. By feeding on vegetation and disturbing the ground as they moved, these animals helped keep parts of the landscape open.

Their activities created opportunities for grasses, wildflowers, and other plants that might otherwise have struggled beneath dense tree cover.

This constant interaction between animals and vegetation helped sustain a diverse mixture of habitats, providing suitable conditions for many different species.

Modern Europe, however, is missing much of this ecological influence. Many of the large wild herbivores that once shaped its landscapes have disappeared, and traditional grazing practices have also declined.

"The ecosystems we see in Europe today lack the large wild herbivores that not only shaped landscapes but also sustained its biodiversity for millions of years. The most dramatic shift has largely taken place within the last hundred years, when traditional extensive grazing disappeared from large parts of the landscape," says Czyzewski.

This loss of grazing pressure has changed how vegetation develops across much of the continent, helping explain why present-day European ecosystems differ so dramatically from those of the distant past.

Europe's Ancient Woodlands Were Full of Wildflowers

The research also offers a different perspective on species commonly associated with farmland and other human-managed environments.

Birds such as larks and jackdaws, along with mammals such as the European hamster, are often regarded as characteristic of agricultural landscapes. Yet the researchers suggest that their evolutionary histories likely extend back to the open woodland environments that existed long before modern farming.

Even familiar wildflowers have connections to these ancient ecosystems.

Wild poppies, now frequently seen growing in agricultural fields, also thrived in areas where large grazing animals disturbed vegetation within ancient woodlands.

These findings challenge the sharp distinction between "forest" and "open habitats" that often guides conservation planning today.

In Europe's ecological past, trees, meadows, shrubs, and grazing animals were not necessarily separate parts of nature. They frequently existed together, forming interconnected habitats that supported a wide range of wildlife.

Why Planting More Trees May Not Always Help Nature

The findings arrive as European countries continue expanding forests to capture carbon dioxide, address climate change, and restore biodiversity.

Although forests can provide important environmental benefits, the researchers argue that planting large areas of uniformly dense woodland may not be the best approach when the goal is to restore Europe's native ecosystems.

Many European species evolved in landscapes containing a mixture of trees and open areas. Converting these habitats into continuous closed-canopy forests could therefore reduce the variety of environments available to wildlife.

The study suggests that restoration efforts should focus more strongly on maintaining diverse landscapes, including open grasslands, scattered woodland, and areas shaped by natural grazing.

"Instead, restoration efforts should place greater emphasis on creating and maintaining mosaics of woodland and open habitats - not least through the restoration of natural-living large herbivores," Svenning concludes.

The findings add to a growing body of research from the same scientific group suggesting that large animals played a far greater role in shaping Europe's ecosystems than previously recognized.

They also reinforce the idea that Europe's ancient landscapes were generally brighter, more open, and more varied than the dense primeval forests often depicted in popular imagination.

Rather than restoring nature by simply planting more trees, the researchers suggest that protecting biodiversity may require recreating the complex balance of woodlands, meadows, and grazing animals that shaped the continent for millions of years.

The familiar image of Europe as a vast, dark, unbroken forest may be deeply rooted in our understanding of nature, but millions of years of evidence are painting a very different picture.

#757. Amanda Seyfried Eager to Campaign for ‘You Can See Everything’ as Awards Eligibility Comes Into Focus (Exclusive)

In her first one-on-one interview about the film, the actress, who could become the only person ever nominated at a major award show for a performance in a documentary, says she's excited to hit the trail: "I’m very proud of the film, so I’m fully ready to engage in that."

Can Amanda Seyfried receive awards recognition for her acclaimed portrayal of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s blockbuster documentary You Can See Everything? No performance featured in a doc has ever been nominated by any major awards group. Many weren’t even sure it was possible. Now, the major awards groups have made their determinations, and The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively report their (split) decisions.

Seyfried has been deemed eligible for a best supporting actress nom by the Critics Choice Awards — but ineligible at the Golden Globe, BAFTA and Actor awards. SAG-AFTRA, which is behind the Actor Awards, encouraged A24 to file a formal appeal to try to qualify Seyfried, but insiders say no appeal will be forthcoming. The studio is focused on an Oscar nom. Related Stories Movies You Can't See Everything: The Sneaky Problem With the Elizabeth Holmes Movie Movies Amanda Seyfried Feared 'You Can See Everything' Could "Destroy" Her Career, Says Her Opinion of Billy Evans "Only Got Worse"

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ submission deadline is today, after which the executive committees of its various branches will begin to review submissions. Official determinations will go out in early December. But in the meantime, THR has learned that A24 has been given assurances by representatives of its Actors Branch Executive Committee that there is no reason to believe that she won’t be okayed.

Per the Academy’s rules governing the best documentary feature Oscar, “Films submitted in this category may also qualify for awards in other categories if they meet the specified requirements.” And per the organization’s rules for acting awards, “The Actors Branch Executive Committee shall have the right and responsibility to resolve all questions of eligibility.” In other words, it’s up to the Actors Branch Executive Committee, which has previously deemed eligible acting noms in docs for those who received on-screen credits, as Seyfried did — and they have no incentive to block their constituents from having the option of voting to nominate someone.

In her first one-on-one interview about the film, Seyfried — who landed an Oscar nom for 2020’s Mank and came close to another for 2025’s The Testament of Ann Lee — tells THR that she’s excited to hit the campaign trail and promote not only her performance but the film itself, which could land another nom in a category that has never previously recognized a doc: best picture. “Now that they’re going to let me loose and show up, I’m down!” Seyfried says.

You Can See Everything blends traditional doc techniques with reenactments featuring Seyfried. The film is at 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes and recently became only the fourth documentary to ever top the domestic box office. It has grossed more than $80 million worldwide and is still playing in nearly 2,500 theaters. Last Sunday, it swept the Critics Choice Documentary Awards. And Fielder and Oppenheim are currently in the U.K. participating in a slew of post-screening Q&As for Academy and British Academy members — including one moderated by Olivia Wilde — that have drawn the likes of Richard Curtis, Cate Blanchett, Riz Ahmed, Barbara Broccoli and Alex Garland.

In our conversation, below, Seyfried reveals when she first realized the film might have legs and that she‘s fully prepared for the demands of an Oscar race. “A campaign is a lot,” she says, “It’s time-consuming. It takes all your energy. And I’m totally willing to do it.”

Amanda, you’ve been in awards contention several times — we spoke when you were in the running for Mank, Long Bright River and The Testament of Ann Lee. When you were shooting those projects, I suspect you realized you might wind up in the awards conversation, no? Was that also the case with You Can See Everything?

With Ann Lee maybe, because I thought it was so special and weird, and special weird movies get some kind of halo effect sometimes. But I usually have low expectations because I don’t want to get disappointed. With You Can See Everything, I didn’t even know if it was ever going to come out! They [Fielder and Oppenheim] were searching for the story. They said very early on that A24 was like, “See what happens. And if nothing happens, that’s okay.”

I was at that surprise first screening of You Can See Everything at the Telluride Film Festival on Sept. 6. You were out of the country promoting another movie. How did you first learn that people who had seen the film were flipping out for it and for your contributions to it?

I was in Venice and only found out hours before I went to bed that they were screening the movie in Telluride. I had thought [Oppenheim] were going to Telluride to screen Primetime [Oppenheim’s other 2026 film], so I was as aware as everybody else was. Later Nathan was like, “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you.” I was like, “I don’t care, it’s all good news.” They’re super discreet for a reason, and I totally respect that.

Nathan had screened it for me months before, and I was like, “Okay, cool. I mean, maybe it’ll come out.” Nobody really knew. So when I found out before I went to bed in Venice that it was screening in Telluride, I got really nervous and excited, because I knew it was industry people. And then I woke up to all this chatter and texts from people involved in the movie, and it was that day that I realized that this was going to be kind of an event piece, something that gets under people’s skin. Whether you love it or not, you’re still thinking about it.

People have been trying to figure out how to describe and recognize your work in the film. It has prompted interesting conversations: “Is the film a documentary? Is what you do in the film a performance? How can there be a performance in a documentary? Is it possible to nominate a performance in a documentary?” My question for you: Do you see it as a performance?

Yeah, I do. The reenactments were definitely a challenge. But it’s not like I ever considered that I would be up for any kind of accolade. I understand the politics and the luck and the timing of awards stuff. I don’t really know if we can fully consider it a doc — it’s very genre-bending. I have seen a lot of documentaries, but not enough to know if they’ve ever done anything like this. I know people have said they have never seen anything like it.

I didn’t see the reenactments as anything very special when I watched it — I thought the movie was interesting — but what I have come to understand from actors who I really respect is that the reenactments feel seamless to people after having spent 100 minutes with Elizabeth Holmes. I come in to the film and I’m able to be myself and to have an opinion and to question Nathan — and also to then just disappear by the end in the prison scene. The fact that actors who I respect and love have said that they’ve experienced it almost as if it’s her is the most incredibly flattering thing I’ve ever experienced, and that makes me feel very good. And there are so many actors that want to talk to me about the film, which is so fun because I would talk shop all day!

The experimental feeling that I got when I was part of it and when I was watching it — I feel like that’s why everybody’s talking about it! Does it necessarily need to be celebrated in every way in awards season? No, it’s being celebrated already. But do people want to challenge the awards structure? Probably.

Whether or not the Academy’s documentary branch embraces the film, it seems like a lot of other people in other branches of the Academy love the film and want to recognize it, and A24 seems to be going full-speed-ahead with an unconventional kind of a campaign that will court that sort of recognition. How much of that are you open to being a part of?

I’m fully present for that. I think the amount of events and the amount of presence you need to have when campaigning for these things is pretty extreme — you saw me go through it last year — but it’s still all very positive because getting a seat at the table is the thing. It’s not necessarily about the win, it’s about getting a seat at the table — even quite literally at The Hollywood Reporter roundtable, or stuff like that.

We’re so glad that you’ll be part of that, by the way. Thank you.

Oh, God, yeah, for sure! Put me in a room with other actors and I’m very happy. A campaign is a lot. It’s time-consuming. It takes all your energy. And I’m totally willing to do it. A24 is great. They’re excited, and I’m very proud of the film, so I’m fully ready to engage in that. And I love these filmmakers! I had a great time with this tiny crew. And I think because [the experience] is so rare, and it will never happen again, I’m doubled-down on it.

That doesn’t mean I’m going to do everything I did last year, because I’ve had a year, an interesting year personally [Seyfried and her husband, Thomas Sadoski, who are the parents of two children, announced in September that they have separated], and as grateful as I am that I am where I am, my priorities are pretty clear. The fact that they [A24] didn’t need me to be involved in the press up until this point has been a godsend, because I’ve been needing to be home.

But I’ll do what I need to do because I support the movie and I support the fact that it is unconventional and I want this to proliferate, if that makes sense? I want [Hollywood] to keep being brave. I want to be part of something that inspires actors to take risks, because yeah, I didn’t know what I was getting into, but I had trust in a few people, and then ended up in a project that changed my life.

I’ve been working for a long time, but I’m having an extraordinary experience with You Can See Everything. It’s just following me around, and it’s great, it’s so fun. I like to talk — you’ve seen me — about stuff that I’m crazy about. And so now that they’re going to let me loose and show up, I’m down!

#756. When do Black Friday sales actually start? Official sale times for Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target

If all the emails flooding your inbox weren't enough of an indication, we're closing in on the biggest shopping holiday of the year. Black Friday technically doesn't happen until the dishes from Thanksgiving are scrubbed and put away. But retailers have gotten antsy over the years, kicking off their sales days or weeks in advance. Heck, the whole month of November is basically Black Friday at this point.

If you're hoping to do some discount shopping this holiday season, knowing precisely when to shop each major retailer's official Black Friday sale is key. To help you best strategize this season, we've rounded up the essential dates and times below.

Black Friday always lands on the day after Thanksgiving and the fourth Friday in November. In 2026, that happens to be on Friday, Nov. 27.

As you've probably noticed, however, most major retailers began rolling out early Black Friday deals as soon as the calendar switched to November. Likewise, some will draw things out even longer with Black Friday discounts that last far past the official shopping holiday. Black Friday is no longer a single 24-hour extravaganza; it's a full season.

Cyber Monday, the more online-centric shopping holiday, falls on the Monday after Black Friday. In 2026, that's on Monday, Nov. 30. Most retailers shift into Cyber Monday mode by the Saturday after Black Friday. It's silly, really, but the lines between the two deal-shopping holidays have been blurred beyond recognition.

Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target tend to have the biggest Black Friday (and Cyber Monday) sales each year, so we've broken down all the nitty gritty details you need to know about each retailer's specific schedule in 2026. Plenty of deals are already live, but if you want to shop the official sales, here's the scoop.

For the second year in a row, Best Buy kicked off its holiday schedule scary early, with its first round of "doorBOOsters" dropping the day before Halloween. The electronics retailer will release new doorbusters on select tech every Friday leading up to the big day.

Best Buy's official Black Friday sale, aka the main event, will run in stores and online from Thursday, Nov. 19 through Saturday, Nov. 28. The calendar then flips to Cyber Monday on Sunday, Nov. 29 and runs through Monday, Nov. 30.

Best Buy's brick-and-mortar stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time on Black Friday. Want an old-school Black Friday experience? You can camp out at stores if you want to score high-demand items, but Best Buy will employ a ticketing system for customer and employee safety.

All Best Buy stores will be closed on Thanksgiving Day.

Walmart announced plans for three major Black Friday calendar events for 2026. The first is an Early Black Friday Sale, which will take place from Nov. 12 through Nov. 15. The main event, aka the official Black Friday deals event will kick off Monday, Nov. 23 and last through Sunday, Nov. 29. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Deals will be live online only from Nov. 23 through Nov. 26, so in-store shoppers will have to wait until Black Friday proper. Walmart's Cyber Monday sale will take place from Monday, Nov. 30 through Wednesday, Dec. 2 online only.

During both the early and official Black Friday events, select online-only deals will be reserved for Walmart+ members exclusively for the first 24 hours, while supplies last. If you're not a Walmart+ member and want early access to these doorbusters, you can sign up for $12.95/month or $98/year. Trial members are not eligible for early access.

Walmart stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time on Black Friday. They'll be closed on Thanksgiving Day.

Target launched its first holiday savings event on Nov. 5, with early deals on holiday decor, kitchen appliances, and toys. Its Deal of the Day program also kicked off on Nov. 1 and will run through Dec. 24. Shoppers can score a new featured deal every day of the week until Dec. 24. So far, we've seen 50% off Stanley tumblers and $30 off Apple AirTags.

The official Black Friday shopping event, however, has not properly been announced. If Target follows a similar schedule as last year, we speculate that it'll kick off on Sunday, Nov. 22, and run through Saturday, Nov. 28. The best deals will likely drop exclusively from Nov. 26 through 28 for Black Friday proper. We'll update this with the latest information once it's revealed.

Target Circle 360 members will likely get early access to select deals, as in years past. The savings season will wrap up with Target's Cyber Monday Event from Nov. 29 through Nov. 30 (most likely), featuring online-only deals.

In 2025, Target made the in-store shopping experience worth it by offering the first 100 guests in line a free limited-edition iridescent tote bag, some with gifts inside valued up to $350. We'll be on the lookout for an in-store shopping incentive this year — stay tuned.

Target stores will open at 6 a.m. local time on Black Friday. Closing times vary by location (check your local store). They'll be closed on Thanksgiving, as is company policy.

As in years past, Amazon is hosting a "Black Friday Week" savings event that will kick off on Thursday, Nov. 19 at 3:01 a.m. ET and run through Cyber Monday on Nov. 30. Banners will probably change over from Black Friday to Cyber Monday on Saturday, Nov. 28.

Daily themed deals will drop throughout the event, with "double drops" on Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper at 3 a.m. and 11 a.m. ET.

You don't need to be a Prime member to shop Amazon's Black Friday sale, but it certainly doesn't hurt. There will likely be Prime-exclusive discounts sprinkled here and there throughout the event.

Amazon will also air its fourth annual Black Friday NFL game on Nov. 27 via Prime Video. (The Pittsburgh Steelers host the Denver Broncos, with kickoff slated for 3 p.m. ET) New discounts on toys, electronics, and apparel will be up for grabs during the game. Fans can shop simultaneously as they watch with an enhanced "Shop the Game" experience. There will also be an NBA on Prime doubleheader to follow (Miami Heat vs. New York Knicks and Los Angeles Lakers vs. San Antonio Spurs).

Christina Buff is a Nashville-based freelance writer for who covers shopping with a splash of entertainment. If you’re ever wondering what streaming service you need to watch something (and the cheapest way to sign up for it), she’s your girl.

Christina received a B.S. in Business Communication (concentration in writing) from Stevenson University and began her professional journey writing and editing press releases. Since then, she’s written content for a marketing agency, blogged for celebrities, and covered local news, politics, women’s lifestyle, fashion, beauty, and just about everything in between for various publications.

When she’s not writing, she’s probably enjoying live music, studying human design, or embroidering and upcycling clothes. You can follow her on Instagram at @touchinfinity.

#755. The 10 Best Luggage Brands For Your Next Adventure

Travel in style with today’s top suitcases, as carried by Elle Fanning, Julianne Moore and more jet-setting stars.

By Natalie Alcala, Danielle Directo-Meston, Erin Lassner November 12, 2026 3:51pm

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission.

Given that airport travel can feel like an overwhelming chore, we’re always looking for new ways to elevate the experience. Whether it’s channeling our inner Rihanna by wearing silky Public Pajamas or treating ourselves to a fresh pair of comfy kicks, it’s all about those tiny touches that make traveling easier.

Updating your luggage lineup is another instant confidence booster that’ll streamline your traveling experience and keep your stuff organized. Here, we’ve rounded up some of the best luggage to take on your next adventure, from Gigi Hadid’s go-to Rimowa statement piece to Shay Mitchell-founded Béis. Related Stories Lifestyle Our Top 29 Holiday Gifts of 2026 Lifestyle The Top 23 Holiday Gifts for Movie Lovers, From Retro Collectibles to Modern Tech

For only $130, Quince’s roomy polycarbonate shell carry-on has 360-degree spinner wheels, a sturdy aluminum telescopic trolley handle with soft rubber for comfort, interior compression panels, TSA-approved locks and a removable laundry bag. For the serious traveler with a little extra cash to spend, we suggest Tumi, more specifically Tumi’s Extended Trip collection, lugged by tastemakers including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. We love the instantly iconic contoured shell and this washed yellow colorway (although it’s also available in black).

Ready for anything, this durable and expandable rolling suitcase’s design also incorporates recycled materials, making this both a sleek and sustainable choice. Tumi has a “worry-free” first-year warranty that covers damages during your first 12 months of ownership; from years two through five, it will repair manufacturing defects and normal wear and tear.

One of the best luggage brands with a lifetime guarantee, Away is known for revolutionizing the suitcase game with its affordable luxury travel essentials through a direct-to-consumer business model. We’re fans of the versatile Carry On, as seen with famous travelers including Lily James and Irina Shayk. Available in a plethora of great hues, this hard shell is Away’s signature style, but if luggage with a soft exterior is more your speed, be sure to check out Away’s first-ever Softside Luggage collection.

Related: The 42 Best Gifts for All Types of Travelers, From Luxe Flight Essentials to Road Trip Gadgets

Launched by Shay Mitchell in 2018, Béis has since taken the travel world by storm. One favorite from the collection is this 21-inch carry-on, available in a range of glossy and matte colorways and boasting over 10,000 five-star reviews.

Key touches include a trolley handle with a cushioned, silicone grip, an interior that expands an extra two inches, plus a logo retractable bag attach strap that holds up to 15 additional pounds. Béis covers damages and defects outside of regular wear and tear with its limited lifetime warranty.

Celebrity hair guru Jen Atkin is no stranger to style, which is why many followed her to Calpak when she collaborated with the brand on a bestselling pink carry-on a few years back. While that collab has sold out, you can still snag this similar colorway in Calpak’s beloved soft-sided luggage made with recycled materials.

The fashionable Bellagio Spinner includes an ergonomic three-position adjustable handle, matching shell, interior lining with Herringbone patterned divider and a protected water-repellent zip with TSA-approved combo locks. The leather trimming details give this case that high-end feel. Bric’s covers its wheeled products under a five-year warranty.

A travel essential of Emmy-winning star Marisa Tomei, Briggs & Riley’s Baseline Essential carry-on boasts the brand’s convenient one-touch CX expansion buttons that instantly increases your packing capacity. The built-in tri-fold garment folder lets you pack away one to two suits sans wrinkles, and two mesh lid zip pockets let you organize your stuff as efficiently as possible. On top of all of that, it’s covered under the brand’s unconditional lifetime guarantee, which means your bag will be repaired free of charged if it gets damaged or breaks (“no proof of purchase needed, no questions asked,” says the company.)

Rimowa is the crème de la crème of high-end luggage, becoming an absolute travel essential for on-the-go stars, including Julianne Moore, Kylie Jenner, Elle Fanning, Cara Delevingne and Jessica Alba. Gigi Hadid has been spotted with Rimowa’s Essential Cabin style a few times, no doubt appreciating its distinctive look and the lighter weight polycarbonate (over the classic aluminum).

Beyond this model, Rimowa offers multiple color and design options, including that signature aluminum exterior for added durability and luxury. Plus, the brand covers all products under a limited lifetime warranty.

Few companies do leather bags quite as well as Dooney & Bourke, and the Connecticut-based accessories brand delivers on all fronts with its classic Florentine Leather Duffle Bag. As the name suggests, this unisex weekender is crafted from soft and supple Italian leather, with brushed gold-tone hardware and reinforced stitching. Measuring 21.5 by 13.5 inches in size, the bag is roomy enough for your clothes, shoes and toiletries, while small enough to throw in the backseat for a road trip, or in the overheard compartment on the plane.

What we like: interior and exterior pockets keep your essentials safely organized, while an included strap lets you wear this over the shoulder. Everything is made with exquisite attention to detail, from the handle wrap and tiny “feet” on the base (to prevent the bag from sitting on the floor) to the leather tanning process, which ensures remarkable depth of color while creating a beautiful, time-honored patina. Suitcases may be more common these days, but Dooney & Bourke’s duffle makes a case for carrying it old school.

The Freeform collection by Samsonite is the company’s ultra lightweight line, and has been updated with a more streamlined panel, an increased packing capacity and a double wheels design to increase maneuverability. Samsonite also offers a 10-year warranty, even though its products are acclaimed for their extreme durability.
