#754. Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy

Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a new type of immune cell therapy that activates only after entering the brain, allowing it to attack cancer while remaining inactive elsewhere in the body.

In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells successfully eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that spreads into surrounding healthy tissue. The treatment also provided lasting protection. When researchers introduced cancer cells again several weeks later, the immune cells continued fighting and prevented new tumors from developing.

DMG is among the most difficult childhood cancers to treat. It grows into the brainstem, a critical region that regulates breathing, heartbeat, and swallowing. Nearly all children diagnosed with the disease die within a year, and existing treatments have had little success in stopping its progression.

The experimental therapy, called B-SYNC CAR-T, could offer a new way forward. Unlike conventional CAR-T treatments, which have struggled against brain tumors, these modified immune cells are programmed to activate their cancer-fighting machinery specifically within the brain. Researchers suspect this targeted approach makes the cells more effective, although the precise reason remains unclear.

The promising results have prompted scientists to prepare for clinical trials at UCSF Health, potentially beginning as early as April 2027.

"It's been a struggle to make CAR-T cells that overcome DMG without causing unacceptable side effects," said Hideho Okada, MD, PhD, a professor of Neurological Surgery at UCSF and co-corresponding author of the study, published October 28 in Science Translational Medicine. "By limiting B-SYNC's CAR expression to when and where it matters -- in the brain -- we saw consistent, total shutdown of DMG tumors in the lab."

Engineering Smarter CAR-T Cells to Fight Brain Cancer

B-SYNC builds on years of research by Okada and Wendell Lim, PhD, a professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology at UCSF. Their goal has been to develop immune cells that can recognize and destroy brain tumors with greater precision.

CAR-T therapy works by modifying the body's T cells, a type of immune cell, so they carry special receptors called CARs. These receptors recognize proteins on cancer cells and trigger an immune attack. Although CAR-T treatments have shown success against certain cancers, brain tumors have remained particularly difficult to overcome.

In 2021, Okada and Lim reported encouraging laboratory findings with an earlier therapy called E-SYNC, designed to treat glioblastoma, another aggressive form of brain cancer.

E-SYNC uses a molecular sensing system known as synNotch to identify EGFRvIII, a mutated protein found on some glioblastoma cells. When this protein is detected, synNotch directs the immune cell to produce a CAR that recognizes two additional tumor-associated proteins, EphA2 and IL13Rα2. This two-step process proved more effective than conventional CAR-T strategies that rely on a single activation step.

However, the approach had an important limitation. Only about 20% of patients have tumors containing EGFRvIII. Even when the protein is initially present, tumors can lose it as treatment eliminates the cancer cells carrying it. This allows remaining cancer cells to escape detection.

To overcome that problem, the researchers searched for a more dependable signal that could activate the therapy in a wider range of patients.

A Molecular Switch That Activates Inside the Brain

The scientists identified brevican, a protein naturally distributed throughout the brain, as a promising alternative.

They redesigned the synNotch system so that it would trigger CAR production only when it encountered brevican. Once activated, these "B-SYNC" CAR-T cells could search for cancer cells carrying EphA2 or IL13Rα2, even if those cells lacked EGFRvIII.

This meant the engineered immune cells no longer depended on a tumor-specific mutation to become active. Instead, they used a protein associated with the brain itself as the signal to begin their attack.

Although B-SYNC was initially developed for glioblastoma, the researchers recognized that it might also work against DMG. Both cancers commonly display EphA2 and IL13Rα2 on their tumor cells, making them potential targets for the same treatment.

Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Okada's laboratory, led experiments to investigate whether B-SYNC could successfully attack this deadly childhood cancer.

New CAR-T Therapy Eliminates Brain Tumors in Mice

The researchers first administered B-SYNC CAR-T cells intravenously (IV) to mice implanted with human DMG cells.

Some of the engineered immune cells traveled through the bloodstream and entered the brain. Once there, they began producing the cancer-targeting CAR receptors and attacking tumor cells.

Importantly, this activation appeared to occur only in the intended location. B-SYNC cells elsewhere in the body, including those circulating in the blood or present in the spleen, did not produce the CAR receptors.

That was "just as we designed it," Lakshmanachetty said.

The team next examined whether delivering the treatment directly into the brain would produce stronger results. They administered B-SYNC using an intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection, which introduces the cells into the brain's fluid-filled ventricles.

The results were striking. In two mouse models containing human DMG tumors, the treatment completely eliminated the cancer in every mouse tested. Conventional CAR-T cells, by comparison, were unable to bring the tumors under control.

The findings suggested that activating the engineered immune cells specifically within the brain could overcome some of the obstacles that have limited earlier CAR-T treatments.

Immune Cells Keep Fighting Long After Tumors Disappear

Destroying the original tumors was only part of the achievement. The researchers also wanted to determine whether the engineered immune cells could remain active and protect against cancer returning.

Nearly seven weeks after the initial treatment, they introduced another round of DMG cells into mice that had already received B-SYNC.

Every treated mouse rejected the new cancer cells, demonstrating that the therapy's protective effects continued well beyond the initial elimination of the tumors.

Further observations showed that B-SYNC cells remained functional more than 70 days after treatment.

One possible explanation involves a problem known as T cell exhaustion. When immune cells remain activated for extended periods, they can gradually lose their ability to attack cancer effectively. By preventing CAR activation until the cells reach the brain, B-SYNC may help preserve their strength for when they encounter tumor cells.

The researchers believe this could be an important reason why their approach performed better than conventional CAR-T therapies.

"We didn't expect B-SYNC CAR-T cells to necessarily persist," Lakshmanachetty said. "But they are still patrolling for cancer over 70 days out -- and they're still very functional."

With the laboratory results demonstrating both tumor elimination and lasting immune activity, the UCSF team is now working to move B-SYNC into human testing.

Okada, Lim, and Lakshmanachetty are collaborating with UCSF cancer specialists to prepare clinical trials. The proposed treatment will use each patient's own T cells, which will be genetically modified to become B-SYNC CAR-T cells.

The transition from laboratory research to clinical testing is moving relatively quickly, reflecting the encouraging findings from the animal experiments.

The first trial will be led by UCSF physicians Marie Jaeger-Krause, MD, and Sabine Mueller, MD, PhD. Researchers plan to evaluate different combinations of intravenous delivery and direct administration into the brain.

For patients receiving ICV treatment, surgeons will implant a shunt connecting the brain's ventricles to a reservoir positioned beneath the scalp. This system will allow doctors to administer repeated doses of the engineered immune cells without requiring a new surgical procedure each time.

Although the treatment has not yet been tested for effectiveness in humans, its ability to completely eliminate tumors and prevent their return in mice has generated considerable optimism.

"Diffuse midline glioma is a heartbreaking diagnosis for patients and their families," said Mueller, director of the UCSF Pediatric Brain Tumor Center, UCSF professor of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Pediatrics, and co-founder of the Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium (PNOC). "This preclinical data is very promising. Mice with DMG are being cured, and we are incredibly excited to bring this therapy to the children and young adults we care for. This is exactly the kind of innovative approach they deserve."

#753. Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z

Ebengo. D. M. et al. Science https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aej4586 (2026).

#752. Are Audiences Ready for a Johnny Depp Career Comeback?

After years away from studio features, the star returns to the box office fray with Paramount's 'Ebenezer.' Analysts are taking note of his lack of introspective press moments on the tour: "It's a clever — if obvious — strategy."

For many onlookers, it likely seems fitting that Johnny Depp returns to the big screen this weekend to play a man haunted by past mistakes.

Depp has largely disappeared from public life for nearly a decade following allegations of domestic abuse, along with negative headlines surrounding his and ex-wife Amber Heard‘s messy 2022 defamation trial. Depp won the case and has denied any abuse allegations, but his professional path has seen its share of setbacks, including Warner Bros. dropping him from the Fantastic Beasts franchise in 2018 on the heels of the actor losing a libel suit against the publisher of The Sun. He has yet to hit the big screen for a studio project in the ensuing years. Related Stories Movies 'Ebenezer' Reviews Roundup: Johnny Depp's Comeback Gets a Chilly Reception Movies 'Ebenezer' Review: Johnny Depp Gets a Creepily Effective Comeback Vehicle in Ti West's Horror-Tinged Take on Dickens' Yuletide Classic

That is set to change with Ebenezer, as director Ti West‘s feature adaptation of Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol hits theaters Friday. Paramount Pictures, which greenlit the film shortly after David Ellison’s Skydance Media acquired the studio two years ago, releases Ebenezer in more than 3,500 North American locations and projects an opening of $20 million domestically, along with another $20 million internationally. Such a turnout is likely to place it No. 1 at the North American box office, as the other major release for the frame is David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank, eyeing a domestic launch in the high single digits against a $40 million budget.

Adrian Daub, who serves as director of the Clayman Institute for Gender Research at Stanford University, closely analyzed social media reactions to Depp and Heard’s legal battle. He tells THR that many individuals’ viewpoints were based on feeling connected to Depp’s roles during his stretch as a major Hollywood star, and indeed, plenty of YouTubers were rewarded with a bounty of clicks from posts defending Depp and blasting Heard. Many Depp fans likely feel nostalgic for the era in the 2000s when the actor, initially known as a reluctant heartthrob and rebellious Hollywood outsider with Edward Scissorhands and What’s Eating Gilbert Grape, rocketed up the A-list with the 2003 smash Pirates of the Caribbean, which became the first of his three Oscar nominations in that decade.

“When my team and I analyzed millions of YouTube comments around Depp v. Heard, we found that a lot of commenters seemed less swayed by the specific facts in the case and more by a general nostalgia for Depp roles of the early aughts that they felt were meaningful,” says Daub. “Lots of invocations of Jack Sparrow — that sort of thing. It also seems like non-North American audiences seem much readier to move on — so the studio is likely banking on nostalgia, and on the fact that non-English speaking audiences like Depp and didn’t track #MeToo in Hollywood all that closely.”

In his heyday, Depp was among the industry’s highest-paid stars, collecting a reported $50 million and beyond, including backend, for his Pirates sequels and 2010’s live-action Alice in Wonderland. But his track record included box office hiccups even before his relationship with Heard began generating unflattering press, as he suffered critical and financial disappointments with 2014’s Transcendence and 2015’s Mortdecai. Heard’s first allegations of abuse against Depp came in court documents filed just days before Disney released the sequel film Alice Through the Looking Glass, which became a money loser for the studio in 2016.

Notably, a number of Depp’s press opportunities were done while in character as Scrooge, including an unannounced appearance at an unrelated San Diego Comic-Con panel that saw the actor riffing for much longer than expected. As himself, Depp participated in the film’s recent junket and spoke to such outlets as Collider, CBS Mornings, Entertainment Tonight, On Film With Kevin McCarthy and Heart Radio U.K. Paramount has been pleased with data suggesting that audiences want Depp back and that he still holds universal appeal, with the in-character appearances having been intended to remind fans of the way that he has previously immersed himself to portray memorable roles like Jack Sparrow and Willy Wonka.

Earlier this month at the film’s London premiere, Depp hinted at his involuntary hiatus from studio work. When the Associated Press asked him about not having booked a Hollywood film in years, he quibbled about the question’s wording before replying, “There was a bit of a vacation, which is fine,” and then a publicist quickly whisked him away from the reporter.

“Refusing to come out of character in promotional events feels like a form of protection for Depp,” Brian J. Robb, author of the 1996 biography Johnny Depp: A Modern Rebel, tells THR. “It both gives audiences a flavor of what the film might be like and very helpfully protects the star from any searching questions about the recent past. He clearly wants to disappear into the role of Ebenezer, hoping that if audiences respond well to the character and the film, then he will have a chance to secure a more long-term comeback. It’s a clever — if obvious — strategy.”

It doesn’t take a detective, the likes of which Depp has played in such projects as 1999’s Sleepy Hollow, to unearth that his real-life trajectory bears similarities to that of Ebenezer Scrooge, a public figure with PR issues until he gets a chance at redemption. Indeed, Ebenezer’s marketing itself has leaned into this connection, with the first trailer featuring Depp delivering the line, “It’s good to be back.” The film appears to have divided critics, as it holds a 50 percent approval from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, although THR’s favorable review declares that it “fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.”

Depp is set to follow Ebenezer with Lionsgate’s Day Drinker, director Marc Webb’s thriller that is slated for a March 2027 release and also stars Madelyn Cline and Penélope Cruz. If the comeback works, Depp would look to follow the paths of such embattled stars as Robert Downey Jr., who bounced back from his addiction-related controversies to lead the MCU and earn an Oscar, and Mel Gibson, whose headlines for antisemitic, racist and anti-gay remarks preceded his best director Oscar nomination for Hacksaw Ridge, not to mention his work helming the forthcoming high-profile follow-up to The Passion of the Christ. Other ostensibly “canceled” public figures have found ways to pivot, whether shifting to lower-profile work or catering directly to a right-wing crowd.

Ernest Owens, author of the book The Case for Cancel Culture and the forthcoming release Divided We Stan, sees a missed opportunity in Depp’s decision to avoid acknowledging his challenging past.

“I thought it would be a cool narrative that he could say, ‘Look, I was a Scrooge. I was a very misguided person and reflected on it, and I’m a new person, like he becomes in the end of A Christmas Carol,‘” the journalist says. “That would have been an interesting, metaphorical way of talking about the movie and his journey. But you have to actually feel that way. And I think Depp is not someone who actually thinks he did anything wrong.”

With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#750. Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy

More than 100 years after Albert Einstein developed his theory of gravity, physicists have uncovered a surprising possibility hidden within his equations. Their work suggests that gravitational fields can undergo a process in which their underlying structures break and reconnect, allowing energy to flow from gravity into matter.

The phenomenon, known as "gravitational reconnection," bears an unexpected resemblance to a process responsible for some of the Sun's most powerful eruptions. Researchers believe this connection could provide new insights into how gravity behaves under extreme conditions, including during collisions between black holes.

The discovery comes from Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's Departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. By examining Einstein's equations from a different mathematical perspective, they identified a remarkable similarity between gravity and the behavior of electrically charged gases known as plasmas.

Their approach could help scientists uncover fundamental rules governing the behavior of gravitational fields. Such insights are especially valuable in regions where gravity severely distorts space-time, making even the most powerful computer simulations difficult to interpret.

How Gravity Could Behave Like a Solar Flare

The key to understanding this discovery lies in a well-known phenomenon called magnetic reconnection. Magnetic fields are often illustrated using curved lines, such as the patterns formed by iron filings around a magnet or the enormous magnetic loops extending above the Sun's surface.

In a plasma, which consists of electrically charged particles, these magnetic field lines can be pulled, twisted, and stretched. Under certain conditions, they undergo a sudden change in their connections, releasing stored magnetic energy into the surrounding particles. This process powers solar flares and ranks among the most important mechanisms for releasing energy throughout the universe.

"Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration," Comisso said. "When they break and reconnect, they release energy."

The resulting energy transfer can produce extraordinarily powerful events. As Comisso explained, "It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events."

The researchers found that gravitational fields may undergo an analogous transformation. However, gravity operates within Einstein's four-dimensional space-time, which includes three dimensions of space and one dimension of time. This makes its underlying mathematical structure different from that of an ordinary magnetic field.

Gravitational Reconnection and the Fabric of Space-Time

"Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field 'sheets' rather than field lines," explained Comisso. "Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a 'sheet.'"

In this mathematical description, gravity is represented by sheets rather than individual field lines. Just as magnetic field lines can change their connections and release energy, these gravitational sheets can also rearrange their connections under the appropriate conditions.

Importantly, the sheets are mathematical representations, not physical surfaces that literally tear apart. Their reconnection describes a way for the gravitational field to transfer energy into matter.

The researchers arrived at this result by exploring properties of Einstein's equations that are not obvious in their usual mathematical form. Their work builds on an earlier investigation that revealed previously unrecognized restrictions on how space-time can bend, stretch, and change over time.

The new study, titled "Reconnection of Gravitational Fields," was published in Physical Review D, a journal of the American Physical Society. It extends findings from an earlier study published in Physical Review Letters by Comisso, Asenjo, and Maricarmen A. Winkler.

That earlier work identified mathematical constraints that determine which changes in the geometry of space-time are possible. Although these restrictions are built into Einstein's theory, they had not previously been recognized in this form.

"Einstein's equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent," said Asenjo. "By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves."

In their latest research, Comisso and Asenjo investigated what happens when the ideal conditions that normally preserve connections within gravitational field structures no longer hold. They found that those connections can change, producing the phenomenon they call gravitational reconnection.

"Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them," Comisso said. "You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior."

Why Plasma Physics Offers New Clues About Gravity

The breakthrough depends on a different mathematical formulation of Einstein's equations developed by physicists in recent years. Although this formulation uses different variables, it is mathematically equivalent to the original equations and describes the same underlying physics.

What makes it particularly useful is its resemblance to equations used to study plasmas. These electrically charged gases make up the Sun, are used in nuclear fusion experiments, and occupy much of the space between stars.

Comisso has devoted his career to understanding plasma behavior. When he and his colleagues recognized the mathematical similarities between plasma physics and gravity, they realized that methods developed to study magnetic fields could also reveal previously overlooked properties of gravitational fields.

This approach allows physicists to identify patterns and restrictions governing space-time without necessarily solving every part of Einstein's equations.

"It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time," Comisso said. "Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints."

Rather than relying entirely on complex numerical calculations, researchers can use these underlying rules to determine which behaviors are physically possible. This could provide a valuable new perspective on gravitational events that are exceptionally difficult to model.

What Gravitational Reconnection Could Mean for Black Holes

One of the most promising applications involves black hole collisions. When two black holes approach and merge, their immense gravitational fields produce extreme distortions in space-time.

To understand these events, astrophysicists typically rely on massive supercomputer simulations. Researchers specify the initial conditions, calculate how the system changes over time, and examine the resulting behavior.

These simulations help scientists predict the gravitational waves generated by merging black holes. Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time that can be detected by instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which is designed to measure the extraordinarily small distortions produced by powerful cosmic events.

The newly identified rules governing gravitational fields could complement these simulations by revealing patterns that might otherwise be difficult to recognize. They may also help researchers better understand how energy is transferred during some of the universe's most extreme gravitational interactions.

For now, gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical finding. Scientists have not yet established how the process operates in actual astrophysical environments or whether its effects can be observed.

The next step is to investigate gravitational reconnection in specific situations, particularly when black holes merge. Comisso hopes this research will eventually make it possible to estimate how much energy such events release and determine whether gravitational reconnection produces recognizable signatures in gravitational wave signals.

If those predictions can be developed and tested, the approach could offer a powerful new way to investigate the behavior of gravity under extreme conditions, revealing more of the physics concealed within Einstein's century-old equations.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation and NASA.

Materials provided by Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#749. Tyrese Gibson to Star in Sports Drama ‘Under the Boards’ From ‘Home Alone’ Producer Scott Rosenfelt (Exclusive)

The feature is set to begin production next year and takes inspiration from the real-life championship run for Atlantic City High School's basketball team.

Tyrese Gibson is looking to bring an inspirational story of high school basketball triumph to the big screen.

The actor, known for the Fast and Furious franchise, is set to star in writer-director Scott Rosenfelt’s sports drama Under the Boards, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. The indie film is expected to begin production in February.

Under the Boards is inspired by real-life events experienced by the Atlantic City High School’s basketball team from 2003 to 2013 as the squad won its first New Jersey state championships. The film centers on larger-than-life head coach Gene Allen (Gibson) and Jim Schafer, the math teacher with a passion for strategy who becomes the assistant coach. Under the Boards looks to celebrate the athletes, families, teachers and community members who supported the team’s unlikely success. Rosenfelt, who helms the movie from his own script, serves as producer alongside Salomé Breziner. Schafer, Gibson and T’Shaun Barrett serve as executive producers, while Debby Schafer co-produces. Jim Schafer, whose path helped inspire the project, is married to Rosenfelt’s cousin, and the casting process is underway to cast the actor who will portray Schafer.

“This film belongs to Atlantic City,” says Rosenfelt. “Tyrese understands that a coach like Gene is part preacher, part politician and part father to every kid on that bench. He is going to bring that whole community to life.”

Adds Breziner, “It is an honor to bring Jim Schafer’s story to life and to celebrate a community that never stopped believing. I am so excited to be working with Tyrese again, and to be back alongside Scott on a film this close to his heart.”

Rosenfelt’s producing credits include Home Alone, Mystic Pizza, Teen Wolf, Critical Thinking and Smoke Signals, and he directed the film Family Prayers. Breziner wrote and directed Tollbooth and Fast Sofa, and she is currently producing the Billy Zane-led Danger Island alongside Rosenfelt.

Gibson is represented by Kris Heller at IAG and Mona Scott-Young at Monami Management.

#748. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

The molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an important role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

The results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how quickly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

"Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment

Cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog."

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an important part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

Each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

The study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

The changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

The results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

Standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed

Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz said.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits

To build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

The investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#744. Why Quentin Tarantino Initially Fired Mélanie Laurent and Isabelle Huppert From ‘Inglourious Basterds’

"If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them sh**. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period," the Oscar-winning filmmaker said in Jay Glennie’s new book.

Quentin Tarantino is getting candid about his decision to fire Mélanie Laurent and Isabelle Huppert before production began for 2009’s Inglourious Basterds.

The Oscar-winning filmmaker opened up in Jay Glennie’s new book, The Making of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds, about why he feels he doesn’t owe actors “shit,” but owes “my film the best actors I can find.”

The dark comedy war film, set in Nazi-occupied France during World War II, centers on a plan to assassinate Nazi leaders by a group of Jewish U.S. soldiers. However, the plan ends up coinciding with a theatre owner’s vengeful plans to do the same. Related Stories Exclusive Excerpt Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds' Movies Cinemark Won't Screen Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Movie Over Netflix's Demands, CEO Says

Though Laurent was eventually rehired for the leading role of Shosanna Dreyfus, the French cinema owner, Tarantino said her initial “table read was terrible,” so he let her go.

“It wasn’t good enough to be terrible,” Tarantino told Glennie. “The most exciting day of preproduction is for me the table read. That is the closest I get to seeing the movie for the first time. Up until then, it’s just been me reading all the scenes to myself or to a friend … so a table read with the whole cast is so exciting and so important to me. Well, Mélanie was terrible, so I fired her.”

Tarantino recalled Laurent calling him to get her job back, explaining she was feeling under the weather at the time of the table read. A persistent Laurent also planned to show up to set regardless of his decision. “I will fly myself to Germany and put myself up into a hotel. I know you’re busy, but I will wait until you see me again,” she told the filmmaker.

She eventually convinced Tarantino to give her another chance, saying he would “turn the clock back” and “they would return to square one.” However, he wouldn’t fully decide if “she was his Shosanna Dreyfus” until after three days of rehearsal.

Laurent ultimately won over Tarantino, going on to play the lead role. “Let me just go on the record for everybody to know: I love Mélanie,” the director told the author.

“The fact of the matter is, if we were not talking about the making of Inglourious Basterds, I would never think about the table read again for the simple reason Mélanie is my Shosanna,” he added. “She did a wonderful job. But we have decided to dive deep into the making of the movie with this book, and this is an important part of its history. You know, we agreed, warts and all. So, if we had not agreed to talk about the shooting of the movie, it would be out of my mind, and I would never think about it again.”

Huppert was a bit of a different story. After being cast as Madame Ada Mimieux, a woman who provides shelter to Shosanna in Paris, Tarantino fired her when she didn’t show up for the table read.

“She didn’t show up, so fuck it. I fired her,” he said. “I mean, I love Isabelle Huppert — Heaven’s Gate and all that — but there were issues with her contract. It just kept stalling. And then not coming to the table read. Well, we cast Maggie Cheung instead.”

“That invariably happens. As far as I’m concerned, if you’re cast and you are not at that table, I don’t owe you jack shit! You can be fired, especially if I get excited by what somebody else did in your absence,” Tarantino continued. He used Michael Parks being cast in two different roles in his Kill Bill films, replacing Ricardo Montalbán, as another example.

Despite Cheung taking on the role, Tarantino ultimately decided to cut those scenes with her character from the movie.

“Maggie was fantastic in the movie, but you just didn’t need to know how Shosanna acquired the cinema. All we needed was a title card saying Four Years Later and Shosanna explaining that she inherited it from her aunt,” Tarantino explained.

Following its release in 2009, Inglourious Basterds went on to gross more than $321 million worldwide. It also earned eight Academy Award nominations, with Christoph Waltz taking home the best supporting actor Oscar for his role as Col. Hans Landa.

“I have no moral compass when it comes to giving roles to actors: They have to be right. They have to feel like they are right for the world I have created,” Tarantino told Glennie about his approach to casting actors. “I have fired actors in the past. If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them shit. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period.”

#743. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

#740. ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Goes Back to (Before) the Beginning With Its 600th Episode

Showrunner Michele Fazekas breaks down Christopher Meloni's return and the state of the Benson-Stabler relationship.

[This story contains spoilers from the 600th episode of Law & Order: SVU.]

Law & Order: SVU reached a huge milestone Thursday: 600 episodes, a number that only two scripted primetime shows have ever hit before. The cast and crew celebrated with a cake on set during filming and a dinner afterward — and then went back to work. Six hundred episodes is an extremely rare feat for a scripted series (The Simpsons and Gunsmoke are the only ones with more), but Thursday’s episode was also the sixth of season 28; 15 more are still to come. Related Stories Business Fanatics Studios' Next Big Media Play Is the NBA All-Star Game TV Jason Benetti Will Replace Dan Hicks on Notre Dame Play-by-Play Saturday Following Sudden Passing (Exclusive)

“That’s just doing television,” showrunner Michele Fazekas told The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s our 600th episode, but it’s also just an episode within 21 episodes [this season]. You’re working on five episodes at the same time at any given moment — you’re in prep on some episodes, you’re writing on some episodes, you’re in post on some episodes. Nothing changed in that regard.”

Titled “Obedience,” the 600th episode brings Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni) back to the Special Victims Unit after jury consultant Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron, who also appeared in the season premiere) convinces Benson (Mariska Hargitay) to take another look at an old case. Gwen is convinced the man in prison for the crime, the rape and murder of a young nun in 1998, is innocent.

Stabler is reluctant to revisit the case — with good reason, it turns out. He failed to follow a couple of leads that could have pointed to the real culprit, a now-retired priest who led mass at the convent where the victim lived. He also cut Benson out of the interrogation in the case, which she went along with at the time because she was new to the squad. The case stirs up complicated feelings in the former partners; when Stabler asks Benson why she’s so interested in digging up the case, she retorts, “Why aren’t you?”

He eventually agrees to work with her, and the pair head upstate to question people who knew the victim (most notably, guest stars Laura Innes and Kathleen Chalfant) and track down the priest.

Fazekas, who wrote the episode (Brenna Malloy directed), said she wanted to give the 600th show the feel of “an old school Benson and Stabler episode” while also looking at the people they have become in the years since. To that end, the episode’s final scenes will give viewers plenty to discuss.

Fazekas unpacked those scenes, the reasons for going back to the show’s early days and more in an interview with THR.

Given the milestone that this is, was there extra planning that went into it? Or did you have ideas on the board for longer than you might normally?

Probably a little bit. I think I had an idea early on in the in the season of what I wished to do, and one of the first things was saying, “Can we bring back Chris Meloni?” Assuming that this is the last centennial episode that we were going to have, it feels like if we could do it, this would be the time to do it. So yeah, there were some earlier ideas than your typical running around trying to figure out what an episode is.

Having Stabler come back into the squad was always part of the plan, then?

It was for me. There were a lot of things that had to happen in order for that to become a reality, including Chris having to be available — he’s busy. But he was. I also knew early on — because I was on the show the first time around, seasons three through seven — I wanted to kind of go back a little bit to an old school Benson and Stabler episode of SVU and honor that era of the show. I just had an idea, and I don’t usually come up with ideas this way, but I was like, “I want it to be a road show.” I want them to be in a car, driving long distances and hashing stuff out. I didn’t know what [the reason] was. I always find that interesting, just putting two people in a place where they can’t get away, and then they have to hash out their stuff.

The structure of SVU is such that cases usually get cleared and some sort of justice is served by the end of the hour. I thought it was really interesting that this one is built on something that they got wrong initially. Why did you want to come at it that way?

In part, it was because you have to explain why are we bringing Detective Stabler back. He doesn’t work in SVU anymore. He works in a completely different department. So what would be big enough that he would come back? It felt sort of organic for it to be an old case, but it’s a case that actually predates the show. The show starts in 1999, and this case is from 1998.

What was not planned but came out in the in the breaking of the story is they were such different people back then. Benson was really new, and Stabler was the senior detective, and she has evolved so much because, at the end of the day, we’re still telling the story of Benson. It fits really nicely into what we’re doing with her character this season, and it made sense for why he’s back. But it also goes to wanting to do and old school SVU episodes, but let’s go back to before SVU was even a thing.

I was also struck by Stabler admitting to Benson that his Catholicism might have blinded him to who the real perpetrator was. His religion has been a thread throughout the character’s run, but I think it’s always interesting when it comes up explicitly in relation to a case.

Chris Meloni was a big proponent of that as well. I think allowing your own preconceptions biases you; it goes to that whole issue [of blind spots] generally. Anybody who was raised Catholic, you think of it as one thing, and it’s very hard for people to accept that this thing that you think is one way has a really dark side. At that time [in 1998], it would have been really hard for Stabler to even understand.

You were on the show for a good portion of the Benson-Stabler partnership during your first tenure, and now you’re back as showrunner. What’s your read on their relationship?

My read is Stabler still has work to do on himself that Benson has done. Benson has evolved in a way, and I love them together, and I love them as partners and as scene partners. But I think part of this episode is talking about how she, in some ways, has moved on from the struggles back then. I think Stabler is still working on it. Stabler is still doing a lot of the same things that he did 20 years ago, and he’s starting to realize, oh, I need to change that.

And given what goes on between them in this episode — arguing about work and life, and then him inviting her to come to Arizona for a while — what do you think the audience’s read is going to be?

Listen, I do think they love each other. I think they both know. I think when he says, “Hey, you want to come to Arizona?” he knows her answer is going to be no. It’s easy to ask that question when you know the answer is no. I don’t think he didn’t mean it, but he also knew what her answer was going to be, and I think now is not the time. Is there time down the line? Maybe, but I think he’s got some work to do. She can have some work to do as well, but I think she’s probably a little further down that path than he is.

I’ve always thought that they love each other in a way that sort of transcends a sexual relationship. They deeply love each other, and they’ve acknowledged that before, and I think this sort of reinforces it. But I also think he knows I’ve got more to do with myself.

Where are you in terms of production now?

We are shooting episode 10 and in prep on episode 11.

Anything you can say about the next few episodes?

We have a nice little arc going of that we started at the beginning of the season that we continue, where the cases that they’re faced with are messy and don’t have easy answers. Benson is really struggling with feeling like nothing has changed. No matter how hard we work, sometimes it doesn’t matter. I like the idea of pushing her — the episode we’re shooting now and the next episode are pushing her to the edges of not even what is legal, but what is ethically and morally right to do, because she’s starting to not care.

The episode we’re shooting right now, the bad guy is so bad. We’re talking about “Why is he doing what he’s doing?” And she actually says, “I don’t care,” which is a big thing for her. But you also understand it because the guy is such a bad guy.

Anything you can say about how Stephanie March re-enters the show as Alex Cabot?

Benson goes to her and asks for help. They didn’t end things on a totally happy note the last time she was on the show, but Benson goes back to her.

Is Alex still doing the same sort of work she was that last time?

#739. Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered

A tiny fish with brilliant orange markings has been discovered in the Brazilian Amazon, but scientists warn that the newly identified species may already be at risk of extinction. Found in a handful of forest pools threatened by human activity, the colorful fish has prompted researchers to call for urgent conservation measures.

The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish. It measures less than three centimeters in standard length, but its appearance is anything but ordinary. Males have rows of bright orange spots along the front half of their bodies, followed by bold orange chevron patterns near the tail. These vivid markings stand out against their pale gray sides.

The discovery was made during fieldwork in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. The research team included scientists from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará, and University of West Florida.

A Striking Discovery in the Amazon Rainforest

The researchers were exploring how different freshwater fish in the Rivulidae family have evolved their life cycles and survival strategies across Brazil's diverse environments. During their surveys, they encountered a fish whose unusual coloration immediately stood out.

"We are developing a research project aimed at investigating the evolution of life-history strategies in freshwater fishes of the family Rivulidae across different biomes in Brazil," said lead researcher Yuri Abrantes of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. "During our sampling in small rivers locally known as 'igarapés' in the Rio Cajari region, in Amapá State, we found this fish with a very striking coloration, which immediately caught our attention."

Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science. The team carefully examined its body proportions, counted its scales, and studied features of its skeleton. They compared these characteristics with those of closely related species and analyzed its mitochondrial DNA to determine whether it represented a distinct species.

"It was an unexpected moment," Abrantes recalled. "Initially, what most caught our attention was the impressive coloration of the males and females, which was unlike anything we had previously encountered in the study area. This sparked our admiration and a great deal of curiosity."

Genetic testing ultimately confirmed that the fish was a previously unrecognized species. For the researchers, the finding was particularly meaningful because it highlighted how much remains to be discovered in parts of the Amazon that are both poorly studied and increasingly threatened.

Once the genetic analysis confirmed the fish's distinct identity, he said, "it was something special, as we saw an opportunity to contribute to increasing our knowledge of Amazonian biodiversity and to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened."

Why Scientists Named the New Fish Laranja

The name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered. In Portuguese, laranja means orange, referring to both the color and the fruit. The name also pays tribute to Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.

"We wanted to choose a name that would highlight a characteristic of the fish while also fostering a sense of connection with the people of the region where it was discovered," Abrantes explained.

Beyond its colorful appearance, the discovery could help scientists better understand the evolution of Amazonian killifish. Some members of this group have developed an extraordinary way to survive in habitats that periodically dry out. Their embryos can stop developing and remain dormant in damp mud, resuming development when seasonal rains refill the pools.

"Laimosemion represents one of the five independent origins of the annual life cycle within the family Rivulidae," said Abrantes. "Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."

Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be Endangered

Despite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain. Scientists have found it in only three small forest pools near Laranjal do Jari, and every known location shows signs of environmental disturbance.

Deforestation, mining, and urban development are putting pressure on the surrounding habitats. One of the pools is close to water that has been discolored by sediment from mining activities. Another is located within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the environment.

The species' entire known range is estimated to cover just 25 square kilometers. Because its habitat is so restricted and faces multiple threats, the researchers believe the fish meets the criteria for classification as Endangered under guidelines established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

To improve its chances of survival, the team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives.

The discovery adds another species to the Amazon's remarkable biological diversity while underscoring the need to protect habitats that scientists have barely begun to explore. Without stronger conservation measures, species such as Laimosemion laranja could face serious threats before researchers have the opportunity to fully understand them.

The study was published in the open access journal Zoosystematics and Evolution.
