#725. ‘Oh, Mary!’ Mania Takes Over L.A.: Director Sam Pinkleton on Bringing the Unruly Broadway Comedy Phenomenon to Full Houses at the Ahmanson

'The play is not what one would call subtle, so it really works in these big rooms. It's also just so fun to be with that many people laughing,' says Pinkleton

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

As most theater fans already know, “Oh, Mary!,” which is as hysterical as it is ahistorical, is the story of possibly unhinged presidential spouse Mary Todd Lincoln, and her thwarted aspirations to escape life in the parlors of the White House for a career in show business. If there is anything Mary would appreciate, it’s a bigger room. So she would be deeply pleased with the production of “Oh, Mary!” that opens this week at L.A.’s Ahmanson Theatre, where the vast majority of seats for its nearly month-long run sold out in advance. That’s not something that happens with every engagement in the 2,100-seat theater, but Mary — and “Mary” — are a unique case, to say the least. Related Stories Patrick Stewart's Final Movie Is 'Avengers: Doomsday'; He Said Before His Death That 'I Can’t Imagine Retiring. I’ll Forever Be an Actor' Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment?

The wild comedic play, directed by Sam Pinkleton and written by (and originally starring) Cole Escola, became Broadway’s toughest ticket immediately upon opening in early 2024, after a smash off-Broadway run. The succession of actors eager to step into Mary’s dress in the last two and a half years has included both drag performers and cis women. On the national tour that is arriving in L.A., the leading lady is the indelicately named drag queen Alaska Thunderfuck, who has some big 19th century shoes to slip into. Even bigger, maybe, since she has a vaster balcony to project to than the one in Broadway’s Lyceum, which has less than half the L.A. theater’s capacity. But in an interview with Variety, Pinkleton suggests that putting “Oh, Mary!” in a larger space might work to the show’s advantage, given the potential contagion of that many ticketholders getting caught up in uncontrolled laughter, as tends to happen as the show grows progressively more outrageous.

Pinkleton is already known to some L.A. audiences for his 2024 Pasadena Playhouse production of “La Cage aux Folles,” and Broadway theatergoers are currently catching his revival of “The Rocky Horror Show” as well as “Oh, Mary!” He also talked with Variety about two other classic musicals he is set to bring back to New York. But first, his thoughts on bringing the thunder to L.A.’s Music Center. (Incidentally, the Ahmanson just announced that the demand for “Oh, Mary!” tickets will result in the show making a return engagement in 2027, for those with FOMO about missing out on the good seats this time.)

Sometimes, when we do a piece about a play coming in, we say something about how we’ll be “helping spread the news.” It might sound silly to say that about this show, though — ust about everyone in L.A. knows that it’s coming.

Well, that’s because there are so many flags on flag poles. It’s like a fascist “Oh, Mary!” state with all of those “Oh, Mary!” flags everywhere.

The tour has been in San Francisco, Portland and Seattle on its way to the Ahmanson. Assuming you must have come out west to see how it’s doing at at least one of those stops, any thoughts on how it’s working as a touring show?

I love this version of the show, and I’m not just saying that because it’s my job to say it to you right now. It’s because we’ve seen the play with so many different people, we’ve kind of learned how it can stretch, and I think that this version of the play is the play. I feel very happy with it. It feels like the play that Cole wrote. It feels like the play that I directed. They’re an incredible company; Alaska is so funny. I was a bit nervous about it in these big theaters, but I saw it in San Francisco at the Curran, and the play is not what one would call subtle, so it really works in these big rooms. It’s also just so fun to be with that many people laughing. So I’m sure that it will curse us because I said this to you, but I feel like it’s going pretty well.

So many of us are curious about how it will feel because you’ve got such a perfect jewel box environment there in New York. But you feel like, from what you’ve been able to see, you get a similar reaction?

Yeah. And you know, the big jump for us was from off-Broadway to Broadway. That was like: What the hell? How is this gonna work in a big theater? Because the Lyceum, the Broadway theater, is small, but it’s very tall, and I honestly thought it was gonna be a disaster on Broadway. I really thought it wouldn’t translate. But I actually think it plays better on Broadway than it did in a small theater. So running it on Broadway has given us the confidence to know how to kind of fill a room with it, and the adaptations we’ve made for the tour, I think, account for the different spaces very smartly.

I also think sometimes it’s easy to kind of insult the audiences at these big theaters. But if you go to the theater in Charlotte, a 3,000-seat theater, that’s your theater. That’s how you experience theater, so the fact that it is at that scale isn’t weird. You know, that’s how I met theater. I grew up in Richmond, Virginia, going to national tours, and I’m sure I saw tiny shows that got swallowed up by that big stage, but it was where I saw theater. So I feel very positive about it being in all of these massive theaters.

Occasionally I go onto Broadway message boards…

…and before I ever got to see the show in New York, I was looking up message threads about “Oh, Mary!” to see whether the reaction was uniformly positive. It was, almost, but there was one discussion that had a header along the lines of, “Am I the only person who didn’t get ‘Oh, Mary!’?” He was confused that everyone in the entire theater was rolling in the aisles except for him. And it made for interesting reading, because a lot of the respondents were basically saying, “Yes, it’s just you… but I really expected there to be a lot more of you. I saw this off-Broadway and loved it but thought it would just appeal to downtowners or the gay comunity.” So people were saying they loved it but they were shocked that everyone else loves it. Obviously you knew that it had a broad appeal, but were you even a little bit surprised at how broad?

I definitely didn’t know it had a broad appeal at all. I think I was on the far side of cynicism there. We made it for a short run downtown, and were delighted that our dumb friends wanted to come, and that was enough, you know? It was like, mission accomplished! We got some gay people to laugh. Hooray! And it wasn’t until we were on Broadway, early on, that I looked around at a matinee and was like, “These people are not gay people from Brooklyn. These people are, like, Aunt Kathy who took the train in and wanted to see a Broadway show.” And Aunt Kathy deserves to have a good time, and God bless her. Aunt Kathy’s laughing at dick jokes, and that felt great. I watched my conservative father watch the show, and he was howling.

I think there could be a lot of explanations for that, but I think at its root, there’s something really old-fashioned about “Oh, Mary!” When people come to me and are like, “It’s groundbreaking, it’s radical!,” I’m like, “It’s actually not. It’s a play with a couch.” I think it’s well-written and I’m very proud of it, but fundamentally it’s a play with a couch, and you’ve seen a play with a couch before. So like I think the elements of it are familiar in a way that make it kind of approachable. It has a bit of Carol Burnett in it, it has a bit of “The Muppet Show” in it, it has a bit of “I Love Lucy” in it. So I didn’t expect it to have the appeal that it has, but I love that it does, and I love, love, love seeing audiences that you wouldn’t expect at this play laugh at some of these jokes. In Hartford, Connecticut, I was like, “How is this gonna go,” watching these older ladies, and they were so into it.

The pure physicality in a few scenes, where the audience in New York was just having waves of laughter, reminded me of seeing some of the old Sid Caesar “Your Show of Shows” sketches from early TV days where the live audience is practically going insane. But that’s part of the rollercoaster ride that the audience goes on, where the audience knows it’s going be outrageous, but it still surprises them with how outrageous.

Yeah. We try to really protect the secrets of it. And part of the fun of it is getting hit with those surprises.

Let’s talk casting. Why is Alaska Thunderfuck so great for this?

Well, Alaska’s known to most as a beloved, famous drag queen, and that she is. But I know Alaska as a great actress. We’ve done a few musicals together, and from the early days when Cole and I started to realize that other people were gonna play this part, Alaska was one of the first names that I brought up. She really can do it all. The thing that is so amazing to me about her is she has this super over-the-top, wacky, absurd public persona. But she is the most disciplined, rigorous performer. There’s no detail too small for her. She works so hard and is such a pro. And she has approached this like a drama — like she’s just a great actress in a drama. It makes it so funny, because she’s 1,000 feet tall and she’s in this massive dress, throwing herself all around, but she’s taking it so seriously.

A lot of people who are fans of the show probably wish that they could see every production of this with every actor, because it’s easy to imagine how wildly different all these Marys would be. It was originated as a role played in drag but you also have cis women doing it. When did you start thinking about how much you could open this up to different types of actors or actresses?

It was sort of a puzzle that was born out of necessity. We really didn’t think much about other people doing it, other than the amazing Hannah Solow, who was originally the standby and went on to take over the part for a while on Broadway. But when we knew that we were gonna keep running on Broadway and Cole needed to take a break, we were like, “Somebody else has to do it.” And Cole and I always took the play very seriously as a dramatic work, even if nobody else did, and so we wanted to make sure the first replacement for Cole wasn’t just a wacky person in a dress. And Betty Gilpin came up, who I think is one of our greatest living actors, and Betty completely got it and approached it like she was doing Chekhov, and it was so, so funny. By having Betty be the first replacement, I think it taught us how good the play is. Then the fun of it has been kind of bouncing… like, making your next move as far from the thing that came before it as possible. So we’ve been able to go from Betty to Jinkx Monsoon to Titus Burgess to Jane Krakowski to… You know, it’s just that Cole wrote a good play, so it can hold a lot.

Just in terms of the sort of extreme turns of the play, which we won’t reveal, I found myself in that tension of wondering if we should identify with Mary, or do we worry that she should be institutionalized immediately for psychosis? Or do we identify with her because she’s kind of psychotic and we have a psychotic side? We go along with her as she acts out in these repressive or strict situations, and it’s not always clear whether to cheer her on or recoil, though it’s understood we’re going to be on her side.

Yeah, I think many of the people who have played Mary… I’m gonna use as an example the great Meg Stalter, who did it on Broadway. The first thing Meg said to me was, “I’ve never seen myself on stage before like that.” And I do think that a lot of the Marys in particular really relate to her, and I think we all can relate to a feeling of being trapped somewhere — a feeling of believing something about yourself so intensely that everybody else thinks is a joke. I mean, I’m not trying to be funny. I do think it’s quite relatable. And there are some things in the play where she gets really honest, and I think on the best of days, those are played with complete truth. So I do think she’s an unlikely hero, but I root for her. Obviously it’s great when people laugh at the play, but I love when people are moved by it. And it can be surprising.

It’s good you mention that, because there is one scene in the play where a lot of us find ourselves thinking, “Wow, this got really kind of earnest for a minute.”

It’s always interesting when things that tend toward outrageousness or even slapstick get briefly sort of serious before the comedy kicks in again. I always think of the movie “Kingpin,” where there is one scene in the middle where the main character talks about his unhappy childhood or something, and there is no laugh in the scene at all — like, “for whatever reason, we’re gonna ground you for just a minute before we go back to being bonkers.” And “Oh, Mary!” reminded me of that. Maybe Mary is an anti-heroine for all of us.

Yeah. I mean, she does outrageous things, but her situation… Maybe being the wife of Abraham Lincoln is not relatable, but I think a lot about her situation is relatable, very broadly.

You said somewhere recently that “The Rocky Horror Show” was your 10th Broadway show. Is that right? That’s a lot.

Somehow that is true. It is my 10th Broadway show.

You’ve had breakthroughs and popular hits before, but as an actual phenomenon, does “Oh, Mary!” feel like the biggest thing in your career at this point?

You know, I’ve had a lot of shows do well. I’ve also had a lot of shows not do well. But what has happened with “Oh, Mary!” and the way that it has kind of caught fire culturally is unique. I’m not a spring chicken, but I’m not on the rocking chair on the porch yet, you know? I’ve got a lot of energy left. And I’ve said to so many people involved in “Oh, Mary!” who have this ss their first Broadway show or their first play, “Guys, it isn’t usually like this. Don’t get used to this.”

So I can see how “Oh, Mary!” is unique in the success of it, but also, the thing I like about my job is directing, and directing is kind of the same whether you’re doing it in a basement in a church in Iowa or on a Broadway stage. So there’s a way that “Oh, Mary!” stands out, and there’s also a way that I just like making shows, you know? I like making shows, and I make a lot of shows, and I’m making a lot of shows right now, and I’m very grateful that “Oh, Mary!” gets to continue to be one of the shows that I’m making.

You’ve had a lot going on, including “The Rocky Horror Show” on Broadway right now, but is there more in the pipeline for you?

I’m doing a lot. I’m opening a musical in London that I love so much it hurts, which is called “Ceilidh,” which is an unspellable word. It’s a Scottish participatory dance musical. I’m doing “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown” at City Center with David Hyde Pierce, Ayo Edebiri and Danielle Brooks, this crazy cast. And then next year I’m going to direct the 50th anniversary Broadway revival of “Annie,” which is kind of a demented cousin of “Oh, Mary!”

Oh, my goodness. I mean, you used the word “earnest” to describe a moment in “Oh, Mary!,” which I really love, and I think that there is an incredible sincerity to “Oh, Mary!” and an incredible exuberance to “Oh, Mary!” I really don’t have a lot of curiosity in things that roll their eyes. I just think the world is cynical enough without us making cynical things inside of it. And so “Annie,” much like “Oh, Mary!,” is just bright-eyed and exuberant and nasty, and it behaves badly, and it’s got teeth. I’m really excited about it. People always think I’m kidding when I say I’m excited about it. I’m like, “No, no, no, I’m so excited about it.” “Annie” is badass.

And what excites you about “Charlie Brown”?

Oh, gosh. I mean, I find the world of Charles Schulz to be so devastating and honest. And “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown” is as if Samuel Beckett wrote a musical. It’s so quietly devastatingly existential and sweet, and not cloying. When I started thinking about doing it with adults, and in particular with David Hyde Pierce as Charlie Brown, I was really moved by the simplicity of it. That’s the whole thing with Charles Schulz: Hpw can you kind of say the most with the least? That is, I think, kind of an amazing challenge to make theater with, and it’s not how I usually make theater. I’m usually kind of a maximalist. And “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown,” by virtue of Charles Schulz, is this invitation to be incredibly emotionally rich and also very spare with how we tell the story. I’m really excited about it. It’s so sweet.

#723. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

#722. Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Giorgia Guglielmi is a freelance writer in Basel, Switzerland.

Both male and female kelp were shown to be capable of reproduction without fertilization.Credit: Madelein_Wolf/Getty

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” says Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, says Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, says Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

The researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

By contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0

#721. ‘Wolfenstein 3’ in Development at Xbox’s MachineGames

“Wolfenstein 3″ is in the works at Xbox‘s Machine Games.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the news Thursday amid Xbox’s 25th anniversary celebration, sharing on X: “Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming’s most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more.”

Sharma also shared a photo featuring a portion of a script for the project:

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more. pic.twitter.com/YyX8LrbTvh

First launched in 1981 by Muse Software and later id Software, the “Wolfenstein” video game franchise is set in an alternate history World War II that largely follow U.S. Army captain William “B.J.” Blazkowicz in his fight against the Nazis. There are more than a dozen games in the series with the two most recent installments being reboots developed by MachineGames in partnership with publisher Bethesda Softworks: 2014’s “Wolfenstein: The New Order” and 2017’s “Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus.”

“Wolfenstein 3” will mark the first game in the franchise to be developed by MachineGames under Xbox ownership following Microsoft’s acquisition of parent company ZeniMax Media in March 2021.

#720. Disney parks launches new app to get you off apps

Going to a Disney park is supposed to transport you somewhere magical, but for many, the experience requires a very rote part of modern life: staring at your phone.

Disney has separate apps for its resorts in California and Florida, as well as those in France, Japan, and China. Booking Lightning Lane appointments (an extra charge that lets guests jump long lines for rides), nabbing meal reservations, and ordering mobile food items all require checking times on the app. It’s something that Disney guests have to do often if they don’t want to wait hours for Space Mountain or a meal at the Blue Bayou restaurant.

Disney brass even acknowledged that its tech-forward approach has lessened the park experience, with Walt Disney Imagineering President Bruce Vaughn saying last year that reliance on the various apps "breaks the spell" of visiting a Disney resort.

Disney’s first experiment to reduce phone use at its parks was revealed this week. The company just launched the Disney Imagineering Labs app (yes, a new app to reduce smartphone use). The first offering of the app is now available to select Magic Key participants (annual passholders) — Secrets of the Spire in Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge. Described by the Disney Tourist blog as an interactive game within the parks' Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge section, the app offers minigames and challenges. It’s not very clear how this reduces phone usage while at the park, though.

The more promising part of the Imagineering Labs app is the Disneyland Enchanted Guide, which does not yet have a release date but is likely to drop early next year, according to Disney Tourist Blog and the Micky Visit blog. The AI-powered app allows text-based and voice-based questions, e.g., "How long is the line at Pirates of the Caribbean?" "Where should we eat at around noon near Tomorrowland?" The most promising aspect of the Enchanted Guide is the ability to set alerts for when a ride or restaurant's wait time drops below a certain time. Rather than constantly checking the app, you can go about your day until you hear that ding from your phone.

As part of the early app rollout, Disney is soliciting feedback from users in-app. Acknowledging that the Imagineering Labs app isn’t a finished product, Disney is asking park power users to weigh in on what aspects of the app truly improve the park experience.

Time will tell if the new app really reduces phone usage at the park. There has been no word on the Disney blogs that the Imagineering Labs app will replace the various Disney park apps, which means you could get an alert on Lightning Lane availability via the Enchanted Guide app and then have to open the Disneyland app to actually book your Lightning Lane appointment. Hopefully, if successful, the apps will be integrated.

Adding to the mixed messages is the partnership between the Enchanted Guide app and Meta for the latter's Ray-Ban smart glasses. Users will be able to pair the glasses with the app, where they can ask the AI about things they see in the park. Again, more offerings can be good, but this doesn’t seem to align with the goal of making visiting a Disney park more of an offline, in-the-moment experience.

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.

Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.

SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

#718. Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky

November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.

#715. Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth

For nearly a century, scientists have considered the possibility that comets helped make life on Earth possible by delivering essential organic molecules from space. Now, new research suggests this long-standing explanation is extremely unlikely.

Comets are known to contain many of the chemical compounds associated with the origins of life. These substances, often called prebiotic molecules, can participate in the chemical reactions that eventually produce the complex ingredients needed for living organisms. For decades, researchers have proposed that comets striking the early Earth supplied a steady stream of these compounds.

However, a new study led by the University of Cambridge challenges that theory. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers found that comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make it extremely difficult for delicate organic molecules to survive. Instead of delivering their chemical cargo intact, most would likely destroy it during their violent arrival.

The findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest that successful delivery of life's building blocks by comets would have been an extraordinarily rare event. Interestingly, the researchers also found that Mars may have offered somewhat better conditions for receiving these molecules, although the likelihood remains very low.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get out of jail free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge's Institute of Astronomy. "It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely."

Why Comets May Have Failed to Deliver Life's Building Blocks

The idea that comets could transport the ingredients for life received renewed attention in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues explored how these icy objects might behave in planetary systems where worlds orbit relatively close together.

Their earlier research suggested that comets could potentially lose speed as they passed between neighboring planets. Through a series of gravitational encounters, a comet might effectively bounce from one planet to another, eventually traveling slowly enough to deliver organic molecules without destroying them.

The team wanted to determine whether a similar process could have occurred in our own Solar System, potentially explaining how essential chemicals reached the young Earth.

"We're learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century," he said.

To investigate, the researchers combined several sophisticated modeling techniques. These included simulations of comet impacts, calculations of how comets interact with planetary atmospheres, and models tracing how comet populations formed and changed as the Solar System developed.

The results revealed a major obstacle. Although a comet might occasionally approach Earth under conditions favorable for preserving organic compounds, such encounters would have been exceptionally uncommon. Successful delivery could not be completely ruled out, but the simulations indicated that it was highly improbable.

A Critical Ingredient for Life Faces Nearly Impossible Odds

To better understand what happens to the molecules carried by comets, the team concentrated on hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a chemical commonly detected in comets throughout our Solar System.

Despite its reputation as a highly toxic substance, hydrogen cyanide is important in research on the origins of life. It contains carbon and nitrogen and can participate in reactions that produce more complex organic compounds, making it a potentially valuable ingredient in the chemistry that preceded living organisms.

The simulations showed that even when hydrogen cyanide managed to survive a comet's arrival, another major problem remained. The impact would need to deposit enough of the molecule in one location to support meaningful chemical reactions. Events capable of producing those useful concentrations were extraordinarily rare.

Timing created yet another difficulty. Comet impacts were much more common during Earth's earliest history, but their frequency declined sharply over the planet's first 500 million years. According to the researchers, there may have been only a handful of opportunities during that entire early period for comets to deliver hydrogen cyanide under favorable conditions.

Even a successful delivery would not necessarily have helped life develop. Hydrogen cyanide deposited on Earth's surface would likely have dispersed or become diluted relatively quickly, leaving little time for the chemical reactions associated with life's origins to get underway.

For the comet theory to work, several unlikely events would therefore have needed to occur together. A comet would have had to strike at just the right speed and angle, preserve its organic cargo, deposit enough material in a suitable location, and trigger important chemical processes before those molecules dispersed.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence - at best, a one-off fluke."

If Not Comets, Where Did Life's Ingredients Come From?

The findings raise a fundamental question about Earth's earliest history. If comets were unlikely to supply the chemical building blocks of life, what was responsible?

One possibility involves asteroids, which collided with the early Earth far more frequently than comets. The researchers suggest that asteroid impacts could have created conditions in which important prebiotic molecules formed through chemical reactions associated with those collisions.

Another explanation is that Earth produced these compounds on its own. Natural chemical processes operating on the young planet may have generated the ingredients necessary for increasingly complex chemistry, without requiring organic molecules to arrive from space.

These possibilities do not establish exactly how life began. Instead, they highlight alternative ways that the raw materials for life could have become available on Earth.

Why Mars May Have Had a Better Chance Than Earth

While the simulations cast serious doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, they also revealed an intriguing possibility involving Mars.

The Red Planet is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere. These characteristics make it a potentially more favorable destination for cometary molecules, since incoming objects could be more likely to reach its surface without completely destroying their chemical cargo.

According to the researchers, Mars may therefore have been better positioned to receive prebiotic compounds during the Solar System's early development, when comet encounters were considerably more frequent.

However, the simulations do not demonstrate that such deliveries actually occurred. Even on Mars, the conditions required for a successful transfer of life's chemical ingredients appear difficult to achieve.

"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn't happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn't happen on either planet."

What the Discovery Means for the Search for Alien Life

Beyond changing how scientists think about Earth's early chemistry, the findings could help guide the search for potentially habitable planets in other star systems.

Future space observatories may be able to investigate distant worlds in greater detail, searching for atmospheric clues that could indicate environments suitable for life. Among the proposed missions is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a potential successor to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The researchers suggest that planetary systems where comets can move between closely spaced planets while gradually losing speed may deserve particular attention. In such environments, the unusual comet delivery mechanism explored in their earlier research could be more likely to operate.

Identifying these systems could help astronomers focus future observations on planets where essential organic molecules may have had a better chance of surviving their journey through space.

Although the new findings make comets an unlikely explanation for how life's building blocks reached Earth, they do not eliminate the possibility that cometary delivery played a role elsewhere. Understanding where these chemical transfers are possible could provide valuable clues as scientists continue investigating how life emerges across the universe.

The research received partial support from the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which is part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!

The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn, shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement.

"We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar.

Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve.

Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth.

The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun.

Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B.

Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea, the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located.

A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#712. Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’

A documentary is a film, too. But at the Oscars, it still hasn’t been fully embraced as one.

One of the breakout hits of the awards season is A24’s insanely entertaining “You Can See Everything” from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which had a surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September and opened in theaters Oct. 16, grossing nearly $80 million at the domestic box office through its fourth weekend. Many professional pundits and awards enthusiasts are predicting the film will make history as the first documentary feature to land a best picture nomination. So we looked at the history of nonfiction films at the Academy Awards to see which movies have been embraced by the various branches and categories (some now defunct) over the years and what that history says about the film’s chances. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — 'Being Heumann' and 'La Bola Negra' Found the Year's Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them? Patrick Stewart Dies: Marvel, Kevin Feige Praise 'X-Men' Icon For Bringing 'Charles Xavier to Life With Grace, Intelligence and Humanity'

Across 98 ceremonies, feature docs have earned a total of 33 nominations in categories other than documentary feature, according to the Academy’s own statistics. Three of them won statuettes.Of the 14 nominations nonfiction films have collected outside their own race since 2013 (the 85th ceremony), 10 have come in best original song.

The documentary feature category is decided by members of the Documentary Branch, which was formed in 2001 and, according to the Academy’s most recent figures, has 719 voting members, making it the third-largest branch behind Actors (1,202) and Executives (759). Preliminary voting runs Dec. 7-11, narrowing the field to a 15-film shortlist that will be announced Dec. 15. Members of the branch will then vote from that list in January to determine the five nominees, which will be revealed Jan. 21.

The Academy has 19 branches, and each nominates within its own discipline. At the same time, the entire voting membership chooses best picture nominees. Although Academy rules do not expressly prohibit documentaries from competing in other categories, nonfiction films rarely factor into races that presume fictional storytelling, including production design, costume design and acting. This year, A24 is pushing “You Can See Everything” in 11 categories, including best picture, director, supporting actress and documentary feature. Its awards site initially listed the film in the artisan races of production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian). However, an updated version of the site no longer lists production design, costume design, makeup and hairstyling or sound. As Variety previously reported, Seyfried’s acting turn is eligible for the Oscars and Critics Choice but not for BAFTA, SAG (The Actor Awards) and the Golden Globes Awards.

No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture or best director. The closest came at the inaugural Oscars, when “Chang: A Drama of the Wilderness” (1927), the jungle drama shot on location in Siam by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack (the duo who would later make 1933’s “King Kong”), was nominated for unique and artistic picture, one of two top prizes handed out that night.

Two years later, “With Byrd at the South Pole” (1930), an account of Richard E. Byrd’s 1928-30 Antarctic expedition, won cinematography for Joseph T. Rucker and Willard Van Der Veer, becoming the first documentary to win an Oscar more than a decade before the Academy created a category for the form. A documentary category was introduced at the 1942 ceremony, with features and shorts competing together. The two were split into separate categories in 1944.

The writers branch took notice in the late 1940s, nominating Robert and Frances Flaherty’s story for “Louisiana Story” (1948), about a young Cajun boy and his pet raccoon and the story and screenplay of Sidney Meyers’ “The Quiet One” (1949), which blends real-life locations with staged scenes to tell the story of Donald Peters, a 10-year-old Black boy from Harlem grappling with severe emotional trauma. They remain the only two documentaries ever nominated for writing, with “The Quiet One” competing in the category then known as writing (story and screenplay).

Norman Foster’s “Navajo” (1952), about a young Navajo boy caught in a clash of cultures, made history as the first film nominated for both documentary feature and cinematography, with Virgil E. Miller cited in the black-and-white category.

The music branch embraced nonfiction scores early on and continued to do so for more than three decades.

Louis Gruenberg’s music for “The Fight for Life” (1940) opened the door, followed by Disney’s wartime hybrid “Victory Through Air Power” (1943) by Edward H. Plumb, Paul J. Smith and Oliver G. Wallace; the Cinerama showcase “This Is Cinerama” (1953) by Louis Forbes; Disney’s True-Life Adventures entries “Perri” (1957) by Paul Smith and “White Wilderness” (1958) by Oliver Wallace; the U.K. import “The Bolshoi Ballet” (1958) by Yuri Faier and G. Rozhdestvensky; and, finally, Gerald Fried’s work on “Birds Do It, Bees Do It” (1975), the last time a documentary score was recognized, more than 50 years ago.

The lone winner of score in that era was “Let It Be” (1970), which took home the original song score for the Beatles, giving the band its first and only Oscar.

Michael Wadleigh’s three-hour music chronicle “Woodstock” (1970) remains the gold standard for crossover recognition. Wadleigh’s concert landmark won documentary feature and earned nominations for film editing (Thelma Schoonmaker, years before her three wins for Martin Scorsese) and sound (Dan Wallin and Larry Johnson). Its three total nominations are still tied with “Flee” for the most ever received by a documentary.

The second editing nomination came 24 years later, when Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams” (1994) was famously shut out of the documentary feature category at the 67th Oscars, even as the editors branch nominated Frederick Marx, James and Bill Haugse. The snub became one of the most notorious in Academy history and helped force a rethink of how the documentary branch selected its nominees.The craft branches have largely closed their doors to nonfiction films since. No documentary has been nominated in cinematography since 1953, in sound since 1971 or in film editing since 1995.

If there is a side door for nonfiction today, it’s the original song category. Twelve documentaries have received nominations for best original song: “Mondo Cane” (1963), for Riz Ortolani and Nino Oliviero’s “More”; “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006), for Melissa Etheridge’s “I Need to Wake Up,” the only song from a documentary to win; “Chasing Ice” (2012), for J. Ralph’s “Before My Time”; “Glen Campbell … I’ll Be Me” (2014), for Glen Campbell and Julian Raymond’s “I’m Not Gonna Miss You”; “The Hunting Ground” (2015), for Diane Warren and Lady Gaga’s “Til It Happens to You”; “Racing Extinction” (2015), for Ralph and Anohni’s “Manta Ray”; “Jim: The James Foley Story” (2016), for Ralph and Sting’s “The Empty Chair”; “RBG” (2018), for Warren’s “I’ll Fight”; “American Symphony” (2023), for Jon Batiste and Dan Wilson’s “It Never Went Away”; “Elton John: Never Too Late” (2024), for Elton John, Brandi Carlile, Andrew Watt and Bernie Taupin’s “Never Too Late”; “Diane Warren: Relentless” (2025), for Warren’s “Dear Me”; and “Viva Verdi!” (2025), for Nicholas Pike’s “Sweet Dreams of Joy.”

Etheridge’s win came more than four decades after “Mondo Cane” opened the door, and “An Inconvenient Truth” also took documentary feature that night. Davis Guggenheim’s climate film remains the only documentary feature winner to also win an Oscar in another category, and it is the last documentary of any kind to win outside its own race.

The more telling number is this one: 10 of the 12 documentary song nominees came from films the documentary branch passed over. Only “An Inconvenient Truth” and “RBG” were nominated in both categories. For distributors of music-driven or celebrity-centered docs, the math is plain. The song campaign is often the more realistic path to the Dolby Theatre than the documentary race itself, as “American Symphony,” “Elton John: Never Too Late” and “Viva Verdi!” (a portrait of Milan’s Casa Verdi retirement home, with its nominated aria sung by Puerto Rican soprano Ana María Martínez) all demonstrated.

The other modern avenue runs through international feature, where a film needs its country’s official submission before Academy voters can weigh in.

Ari Folman’s animated documentary “Waltz With Bashir” (2008) broke through first, nominated for foreign language film for Israel at the 81st Oscars, though it missed documentary feature. A decade later, three straight years of history followed. North Macedonia’s “Honeyland” (2019) became the first film nominated for both documentary feature and international feature at the 92nd ceremony. Alexander Nanau’s “Collective” (2020) repeated the feat the following year and gave Romania its first Oscar nomination ever. Then Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s Danish feature “Flee” (2021) became the first film nominated in documentary feature, animated feature and international feature in the same year.

“Honeyland” lost to “American Factory” (2019) and “Parasite” (2019), “Collective” fell to “My Octopus Teacher” (2020) and “Another Round” (2020), and “Flee” went 0-for-3 against “Summer of Soul” (2021), “Encanto” (2021) and “Drive My Car” (2021). Four ceremonies have passed since “Flee” without another documentary in the international lineup.

So what does nearly a century of history tell us about “You Can See Everything?”

For starters, the doors that have opened for nonfiction have mostly been in craft and music races and those are precisely the categories where A24 has trimmed and focused its campaign. The film has already swept the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, winning all five categories in which it was nominated. But the Academy has been a tougher nut to crack.

Best picture is a different animal. The documentary branch doesn’t decide it. The full voting membership, now more than 10,000 industry professionals, does. That cuts both ways. A film the documentary branch might view with suspicion, as it once did “Hoop Dreams,” can still find support among actors, executives and craftspeople who simply loved the movie. The music branch has already shown that pattern 10 times over, nominating songs from documentaries the doc branch passed over. It isn’t far-fetched to imagine “You Can See Everything” landing in best picture while missing documentary feature altogether, a scenario already being floated this season.

Variety’s latest Oscar predictions have “You Can See Everything” earning three nominations: best picture, supporting actress for Seyfried and film editing. Notably absent is documentary feature, a category in which many pundits believe its omission would rank among the branch’s most significant snubs, alongside such overlooked films as “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” (2018), “Jane” (2017), “Stories We Tell” (2012), etc. But even a fraction of that predicted crossover haul would rewrite the Oscar record books.

The first major test comes Dec. 15, when the documentary shortlist is announced, followed by Oscar nominations on Jan. 21. If “You Can See Everything” breaks through in even one of the Academy’s other races, it would mark a significant milestone for A24.

Because, hey, a documentary is a film, too.

#711. A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds

A mysterious structure stretching roughly 93 billion miles across space is giving astronomers new clues about the violent events that shape young planetary systems. Known as the "Cat's Tail," this enormous cloud of dark material lies about 63 light-years from Earth, in the faint constellation Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"). For the past two years, its unusual appearance and uncertain origins have puzzled scientists.

The structure is part of a vast disk of dust and debris surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star system that resembles our own solar system during its early development. Now, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have captured previously hidden details of the Cat's Tail in visible light for the first time.

The discovery is described in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Led by University of Arizona planetary scientist Arin Avsar, the research team combined the new Hubble images with observations spanning more than 14 years. Their findings provide a clearer picture of the structure's composition, location, and shape, along with additional evidence that a massive collision may have created it.

A Possible Collision Between Pluto-Sized Worlds

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies - think something like Pluto," said Avsar, a doctoral student working with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory.

"Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

The mystery becomes even more interesting when viewed in the context of how planetary systems form.

Today, our solar system appears relatively orderly. Planets follow established paths around the Sun, while many smaller rocky objects occupy "designated" regions such as the asteroid belt. But 4.6 billion years ago, the situation was dramatically different.

A young sun was surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust. Rocky objects repeatedly collided, sometimes breaking apart and sometimes combining into larger bodies. Over time, some accumulated enough material to become planets, while countless others were destroyed or scattered.

Astronomers study younger systems like Beta Pictoris because they offer an opportunity to observe processes that unfolded in our own cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. Its debris disk, consisting of dust and fragments left behind during planetary development, is believed to be approaching the final stages of planet formation.

Why Hubble Could Finally See the Mysterious Cat's Tail

One of the most intriguing questions about the Cat's Tail is why it was previously detectable in infrared light but so difficult to observe in visible light.

The answer may lie in the unusual material that makes up the enormous structure.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

Organic refractory material consists of complex carbon compounds that can withstand relatively harsh conditions in space. Because these compounds absorb much of the visible light that strikes them, they can make the surrounding dust appear exceptionally dark.

The Hubble observations also support another unusual finding: the Cat's Tail appears to be composed of extremely small, surprisingly porous dust particles.

Individual grains measure only about a micron across, roughly one millionth of a meter. Yet instead of being compact and solid, they appear remarkably "fluffy," with substantial empty space within their structures.

The scale of the entire cloud is difficult to imagine. It may stretch as far as 1,000 astronomical units, with one astronomical unit (AU) defined as the average distance between Earth and the Sun. That corresponds to approximately 93 billion miles, or the equivalent of lining up around 200 trillion house cats from tail to nose.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

How a Violent Collision Could Create Fluffy Cosmic Dust

If the Cat's Tail really formed when large planetary bodies smashed into each other, researchers still need to explain how that destruction produced such tiny, porous particles.

One possibility is that the collision was powerful enough to vaporize some of the material involved.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory.

In this scenario, the intense impact would have transformed solid carbon material into gas. As the material cooled, it could have condensed back into solid particles with unusually open, lightweight structures.

However, the precise process remains uncertain, and additional observations will be needed to determine whether this explanation is correct.

A 93-Billion-Mile Structure With an Unexpected Shape

The new research also challenges previous assumptions about where the Cat's Tail extends in space.

By combining visible light observations from Hubble with infrared measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers used computer modeling to reconstruct the structure's possible three-dimensional arrangement.

Earlier observations suggested that the Cat's Tail extended outward from Beta Pictoris and far behind the star from Earth's perspective. Because the surrounding debris disk is viewed nearly edge-on, it was difficult to determine how much of the structure extended away from us rather than across our field of view.

The new analysis points to a different explanation.

"We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat's Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it," Avsar said. "It's essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it."

This suggests the structure may be spread mainly across the sky as seen from Earth, rather than projecting deep into space behind the star.

The revised geometry gives astronomers a better understanding of where the dust is located and could help them reconstruct the event that produced it.

Hubble Discovers a Strange Warp Caused by a Giant Planet

The Cat's Tail was not the only unusual feature revealed by the new observations.

Using Hubble in a different observational configuration, Avsar and his colleagues also identified an unexpected distortion in the broad halo of dust surrounding Beta Pictoris.

The researchers suspect this strange warp may be caused by the gravitational influence of Beta Pic b, one of three planets in the system.

Beta Pic b is a massive gas giant estimated to be about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. Its powerful gravity may be disturbing the surrounding debris, altering the paths of dust particles, comets, and other icy objects across enormous distances.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

The finding highlights how giant planets can shape their environments far beyond their immediate orbits.

A Glimpse Into Our Solar System's Violent Past

For researchers, Beta Pictoris offers more than an opportunity to investigate an unusual cosmic structure. It may also provide a window into the early history of our own solar system.

Consider the Kuiper Belt, the distant region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto and numerous other icy bodies.

When the Kuiper Belt was only about 20 million years old, astronomers believe it was much more crowded than it is today. It may have contained hundreds of objects comparable in size to Pluto.

Over billions of years, the gravitational influence of the solar system's outer giant planets likely changed that environment dramatically. By disturbing the orbits of smaller bodies, these planets may have pushed many objects into new regions or expelled them from the solar system entirely, effectively "clearing out" much of the original population.

The strange dust tail and newly identified warp around Beta Pictoris may offer clues to similar processes unfolding in another planetary system.

By studying these distant structures, astronomers hope to better understand how violent collisions, migrating debris, and the immense gravity of giant planets helped transform the chaos of the early solar system into the planetary arrangement we see today.

Ancient Roman cities, temples and amphitheaters across the Mediterranean will fall into the moon's shadow during the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities.

From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene.

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality.

Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds

Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast

Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning.

Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast

Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins.

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds

Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast

Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. That high sun will require some careful positioning and probably a wide-angle composition, but eclipse photographers will have an extraordinary collection of arches, columns and temples to use as foregrounds.

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes, 23 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 56 degrees above east-southeast

It may be the third-largest and one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, but El Jem offers another reason to consider it for totality. Unlike Rome's Colosseum — which it closely resembles — visitors can explore its multi-tiered seating, climb high into the surviving structure for panoramic views and visit the underground passages once used by gladiators and animals. Built around A.D. 238, El Jem combines one of Rome's greatest surviving monuments with some of the most promising eclipse conditions on the entire track.
